# avoid3_ui

"Avoid 3" on a myCobot 280 Pi: play on screen, against the computer, or with
the arm placing every piece. Adapted from
[tic_tac_toe_ui](https://github.com/cggs-matthew-pham/tic_tac_toe_ui), with
the gravity idea from
[connect4_ui](https://github.com/cggs-matthew-pham/connect4_ui).

## Rules

- 5 x 5 board with gravity: a move is a column (1-5), and the piece drops to
  the lowest empty square in it.
- Make **3 in a line** of your colour (across, down or diagonal) and you
  **lose**. 4 or more in a line also loses.
- A full board with no line is a draw.
- Red goes first. Each player stages 15 pieces (5 stacks of 3), but only
  13 Red and 12 Yellow can ever be played; the rest are spares.

## Running it

```
python3 main.py              # the game (runs on screen only if there's no arm)
python3 test_game.py         # checks the rules, the computer player and move typing
python3 test_mycobot_squares.py   # calibrate the arm (on the Pi, over SSH is fine)
python3 calibrate_zero.py    # only if the joint zeros have drifted
```

Moves can be clicked (anywhere in a column, or its number) or typed: `3`,
`three`, `column 3`, `left`, `far right`, `middle`, `left of centre`. Voice
input only needs to turn speech into text and call `moves.parse_move()`.

Modes: two player, computer easy (any move that doesn't lose straight away),
computer hard (looks ahead as far as `THINK_SECONDS` in `game.py` allows;
2 s by default).

## Files

| File | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `game.py` | Rules and the computer player. Plain functions, same names as tic-tac-toe. |
| `moves.py` | Typed (later spoken) moves to a column number. |
| `ui.py` | Tkinter window. |
| `main.py` | Joins them up. The robot is optional. |
| `robot.py` | Layout, calibration file, gripper/suction, pick and place. |
| `test_mycobot_squares.py` | Calibration tool. |
| `calibrate_zero.py` | Joint zero calibration (unchanged from tic-tac-toe). |
| `hardware/avoid3_sheet_A4.pdf` | The printable board and block labels. |
| `hardware/make_sheet.py` | Makes that PDF. |
| `hardware/board.scad` | 3D-printable pocket board and blocks (same layout). |

## The layout

Print `hardware/avoid3_sheet_A4.pdf` at 100% (page 1 is the board, page 2 is
labels for the block tops). Remake it with `python3 hardware/make_sheet.py`
(needs `pip install reportlab`) after changing the spacing. 7 columns x 5
rows, robot at the top edge:

```
                 ROBOT
   21  22  23  24  25    R5  Y5      ROW 5
   16  17  18  19  20    R4  Y4      ROW 4
   11  12  13  14  15    R3  Y3      ROW 3
    6   7   8   9  10    R2  Y2      ROW 2
    1   2   3   4   5    R1  Y1      ROW 1: fills first
                PLAYER

Everything is numbered from the player's side, like Connect 4 seen from the
front: a block goes in the empty square nearest the player in its column.
```

Rows are 25 mm apart and columns 40 mm apart, with an extra 5 mm before
the Red column and again before Yellow (`STAGING_EXTRA`), so the gripper can
open wider when picking from a stack. The gripper closes
left-right (across the columns), so the fingers never reach forwards or
back and the rows can be close. That keeps the far corners about 250 mm from
the base (inside the 280 mm rated reach) and the nearest row about 115 mm out
(well clear of the base). If your gripper closes towards / away from the
robot, change `TOOL_DOWN`'s rz to 90 in `robot.py`.

Spacing lives in three places that must match: `ROW_PITCH` / `COLUMN_PITCH`
/ `EDGE_TO_TOP_ROW` in `robot.py`, the same names in `hardware/make_sheet.py`,
and `row_pitch` / `column_pitch` in `hardware/board.scad`.

**Set up first:** `test_mycobot_squares.py`, option 4. It:

1. Explains where to put the sheet and asks for your measurement
   (`SHEET_GAP`).
2. Measures the grip height and offset: you hold the open gripper (or cup)
   on a block on square 13 by hand, and it reads where the end of the arm
   is. The arm's coordinates are for its end plate, not the fingertips, and
   the gripper can sit off to one side, so every starting position is
   shifted by the measured difference. Until this is done the tool won't
   travel to spots: a guessed height can send the arm too high and make it
   hit itself near the base. Saved to `GRIP_Z` and `GRIP_ANCHOR` in
   `robot.py`; option 5 measures again after moving the sheet or tool.
3. Moves the arm out towards the two far corners (square 1 and Y1) and above
   the nearest square to check
   it can reach them. Coordinate moves closer than 80 mm to the base
   (`NEAR_LIMIT`) are refused, because the arm folds over itself there.

The sheet is designed for a 60 mm gap: the far corners are then about
250 mm from the base and the nearest squares about 115 mm.

## End effector

`END_EFFECTOR` in `robot.py`: `"gripper"` (default) or `"suction"`.

- **Gripper**: it should never open fully, or the fingers hit the blocks
  next door. Three `set_gripper_value` numbers (0-100): `GRIPPER_PICK_OPEN`
  (a bit wider, before going down onto a stack, so a slightly-off approach
  still gets around the block), `GRIPPER_OPEN` (just enough to let go on the
  board) and `GRIPPER_CLOSED`. Set them with option 6 in
  `test_mycobot_squares.py`: it shows which end is open, lets you try values
  with a block in the fingers, and saves them. Do this before option 4.
  Blocks are taken from the tallest stack first (all the tops, then the
  middles, then the bottoms), so the gripper body never has a stack more
  than one block higher beside it. Coloured labels on top are fine.
- **Suction**: the pump is on GPIO 20 and the valve on GPIO 21, set up
  HIGH (LOW = on). `PUMP_ENABLED = False` by default; tick "Suction pump on"
  in the window, or use `pump` in the calibration tool. Keep block tops
  plain for a good seal.

Calibrate with the one you'll play with. They hold a block at different
heights, so the saved angles aren't interchangeable.

OblongNoodle/OpenLite-Mobile.readme:
# OpenLite Mobile

OpenLite for Android: the OpenSpell game in a full-screen WebView with
OpenLite's plugins, which come from the PC client's `mobile` branch
([OpenLite](https://github.com/OblongNoodle/OpenLite)): PC changes reach the
phone only when that branch is moved on purpose (the PC client's heavier
graphics work stays off the phone).

- `build.ps1 [-Install]` builds the APK (and installs it over USB).
- The app updates its plugins itself: `.github/workflows/bundle.yml` builds
  them from the PC client into a bundle on this repo's GitHub Pages site, and
  the app downloads it on launch (used from the next launch).
- Plugins that don't work on a phone are listed in `scripts/sync-plugins.mjs`.
- OSRS models and textures come from your own OSRS cache, copied to the
  phone; nothing from the cache is in this repo or the app.

commits.msg:
Restart the game's people-sprite worker when it stops answering

The game paints players and human NPCs (bankers, shop keepers) one at a
time in a web worker and waits for each before sending the next. On
Android it can stop answering after the app has been in the background,
and then no new person is ever drawn or clickable until a restart. A
watchdog notices a request that hasn't come back in 6 seconds, starts a
fresh worker and canvas, and sends the request again. The session log
notes each restart and the queue's state on returning to the app.

miguel-apereira/TheGetawayRecomp.readme:
# TheGetawayRecomp

A native Windows port of **The Getaway** (PlayStation 2, 2002) built by
static recompilation. The game's MIPS R5900 code is translated ahead of time
to C++ with [PS2Recomp](https://github.com/ran-j/PS2Recomp), and the PS2
hardware it talked to (GS, VU, IOP, SPU2, IPU) is replaced with native code
on SDL3 and Vulkan instead of being emulated.

> **Status:** early boot, not playable. The recompiled game boots through
> the legal notice, the Team Soho logo and the intro movie to the main menu,
> which responds to the pad. Choosing New Game stops on the first loading
> screen. Next goal: getting past it. See [Progress](#progress).

## Progress

Done, on `main`:

- Host shell: asks for your ISO, checks it is SCUS-97133, extracts it once
  into a `game` folder, and opens an SDL3 window with a Vulkan swapchain.
- Disc tools: ISO9660 reader and `tgr-disc`, which also lists, verifies and
  extracts the game's `PACK_EE.PAK` and `PACK_IOP.PAK` archives.
- Analysis: the stripped boot ELF analysed in Ghidra with the Emotion Engine
  extension, and the function map committed in `recomp/config/`.
- Recompilation: `ps2_recomp` (our PS2Recomp fork) turns the ELF into C++,
  about 46,000 functions, which compile and link into the exe with MSVC.
- The recompiled game runs on its own thread inside our exe, with a
  `--headless` mode for machines without a working Vulkan window.
- Sony SDK functions are named from PS2Recomp's symbol database, so the
  runtime replaces the game's own SIF, CD, pad, memory card, DMA and GS
  library code.
- Native replacements for the game's own IOP modules: `PFS.IRX` (file
  server, reading from the extracted data and the PAK archives) and
  `STREAM.IRX` (sound engine, silent for now).
- A native IPU with an MPEG-2 intra decoder written from the standard: the
  intro movie and the main menu's moving background play.
- The game's picture shows in the window (read back from PS2Recomp's
  software GS for now), with gamepad and keyboard input.
- The legal notice, the Team Soho logo, the intro movie and the main menu
  (New Game, Load Game, Extra Features, Options) work.
- Players no longer need the Vulkan SDK; validation is opt-in with
  `--validation`.
- `tgr-profile`, a sampling profiler that needs no admin rights. In Release
  the game runs at about a fifth of full speed, and most of that time goes
  to PS2Recomp's software GS, which the native GS will replace.

Still to come: a native GS renderer on Vulkan, VU1 microcode, sound (SPU2),
memory card saves, then enhancements. The milestones are listed in
[docs/ARCHITECTURE.md](docs/ARCHITECTURE.md#milestones).

## You need your own copy of the game

This repository contains **no game files**: no ISO, no ELF, no assets, and no
code generated from them. You must supply your own dump of the supported
release, made from a disc you own:

| Title | Region | Serial | Boot ELF |
|---|---|---|---|
| The Getaway | NTSC-U | SCUS-97133 | `SCUS_971.33` |

The PAL releases (SCES-51159, SCES-51426) are not supported: every address
in the recompilation config belongs to one exact executable.

**Players:** on first run, `TheGetawayRecomp.exe` asks you to pick your
`.iso`, checks it, and extracts it once into a `game` folder next to the exe.
Run it with `--reinstall` to extract again, or `--iso <path>` to skip the
file dialog.

**Developers:** also put your dump in `iso/` (for example
`iso/The Getaway.iso`) for the recompilation pipeline. Everything in that
folder is ignored by git. See [iso/README.md](iso/README.md).

## Requirements

- Windows 10 or 11, x64
- Visual Studio 2022 or newer with **Desktop development with C++**
  (includes MSVC, CMake and Ninja)
- Git
- A GPU with Vulkan 1.2 drivers
- Developers only, optional: the [Vulkan SDK](https://vulkan.lunarg.com/)
  for validation layers. Players only need a GPU driver.
- For analysis: [Ghidra](https://ghidra-sre.org/) with the
  [Emotion Engine extension](https://github.com/chaoticgd/ghidra-emotionengine-reloaded),
  and PCSX2 as a reference

## Getting started

From a PowerShell prompt in the repository root:

```powershell
# 1. Fetch the third-party code in external/ at the pinned versions
powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File tools\scripts\bootstrap.ps1

# 2. Build the host shell, tgr-disc and ps2_recomp
#    (Debug by default; -Preset msvc-release for an optimised build)
powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File tools\scripts\build.ps1

# 3. Check your disc and extract the boot ELF and IRX modules to iso\extracted
powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File tools\scripts\extract-disc.ps1

# 4. Turn the boot ELF into C++ in recomp\generated, using the committed config
powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File tools\scripts\recompile.ps1

# 5. Build again with the generated code compiled and linked in
powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File tools\scripts\build.ps1 -WithRecompiledCode

# 6. Start the exe (the first run asks for your ISO and extracts it)
powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File tools\scripts\run.ps1
```

Steps 1 to 3 and 6 alone give the host shell without any game code. The
generated code is large: a clean build with it takes a long while, and the
game runs too slowly in Debug, so use `-Preset msvc-release` to run it
(pass the same `-Preset` to `run.ps1`).

The exe takes `--iso <path>` to skip the file dialog, `--reinstall` to
extract again, `--data <dir>` for another game data folder, and
`--validation` for Vulkan validation layers.

For development, `--headless` runs the game with no window and logs the
guest PC every two seconds; add `--seconds <n>` to stop after a while,
`--press START@70` (repeatable) for scripted pad presses,
`--dump-frames <dir>` to save the picture every two seconds, and
`--threads` or `--watch <address>` for more state in the log.

Visual Studio can also open the folder directly and pick up `CMakePresets.json`.

The full recompilation pipeline, including how to redo the Ghidra analysis
that produced `recomp/config/`, is describe

Play the intro movie with a native IPU

The Getaway decodes its movies by driving the IPU itself (IPUHugeMovie:
FDEC, IDEC, SETVQ, PACK, SETTH, with DMA channels 3 and 4). src/hw/Ipu.cpp
replaces the IPU natively: an MPEG-2 intra macroblock decoder written from
the standard (DCT tables B-14/B-15, DC and macroblock address VLCs,
quantiser matrices, IDCT), colour conversion to RGB32/RGB16 with the SETTH
alpha rules, PACK to RGB16 or 4-bit VQ indices, and the IPU registers,
FIFOs and start/end code handling. The PS2Recomp fork moves to the commit
that routes the IPU to host code.

The game's own libipu now runs against it instead of the runtime's stubs:
recomp/config/SCUS-97133.names.toml renames sceIpuInit, sceIpuSync,
sceIpuStopDMA and sceIpuRestartDMA so the exporter keeps them, and
ApplySceNames.java lets hand-made names override the database's.
sceIpuInit loads the quantiser matrices the movies need.

Two fixes the movie needed in the native IOP modules:
- Stream plays streams for their real length (from the VAG header in
  PACK_IOP.PAK) and reports them playing; the game waits for the intro
  music to play before starting the movie.
- Pfs finishes queued reads at the next call from the EE too, not only at
  vblank; the movie streams more reads per frame than the game has status
  slots.

The intro movie now plays in headless runs.

draws to Vulkan itself.

PadInput turns the first SDL gamepad and the keyboard (PS2Recomp's layout:
arrows/WASD, X/Space cross, C/Esc circle, Z square, V triangle, Q/E L1/R1,

Replace PFS.IRX and STREAM.IRX with native code

The Getaway's two own IOP modules now run as C++ on the host instead of on
an IOP interpreter:

- Pfs: the file server on RPC 0x791. Queued reads by disc sector or name
  come from the extracted game data through disc_layout.tsv, PACK_EE.PAK
  reads by PAK sector, and sound packs from PACK_IOP.PAK by name. Reads
  finish on the next vblank and call the game's EE server back, as the IRX
  did from its own threads.
- Stream: the sound engine on RPC 0x12345, silent for now. It registers
  samples and resident banks the way the IRX numbers them and reports every
  voice idle.

Headless runs gain --watch <address> (log an EE word), --threads (log EE
threads and blocked semaphores) and --dump-frames <dir> (save the GS
display as BMP), and log DMA/GIF/VIF traffic.

The PS2Recomp fork moves to eb98674: host replacements for IOP modules,
EE-side RPC servers kept apart from IOP ones, thread priority 0, and the GS
SIGNAL/FINISH interrupt. With these the game boots to its first screen, the
legal notice, in headless runs.

mjaylove22/urndle.readme:
# Urndle

A daily hero-guessing game for Valve's Deadlock, in the style of LoLdle. Fan project, not affiliated with Valve.

Six modes, each with its own hero of the day (switch with the tabs, or link straight to `#quote`, `#ability`, `#emoji`, `#splash`, `#weapon`):

| Mode | Clue | Each wrong guess… |
|---|---|---|
| Classic | Attribute comparison table | adds a row of green/yellow/red hints |
| Quote | A voice line transcript | after 3, unlocks the audio |
| Ability | An ability icon, rotated | after 3, turns it upright |
| Emoji | Emoji describing the hero | reveals one more emoji |
| Splash | Zoomed-in hero art | zooms out |
| Weapon | Silhouette of the hero's gun | after 3, shows it in color; after 5, names it |

## Run locally

`fetch` doesn't work over `file://`, so serve the folder:

```
python -m http.server 8000
```

Then open http://localhost:8000.

## Test

```
node test.js
```

Checks the daily pick for every mode, the attribute comparison, share text, and that every image/audio file exists.

## Data

Everything except emoji comes from [deadlock.wiki](https://deadlock.wiki). Refresh it with:

```
node scripts/fetch-wiki.js
```

It rebuilds `heroes.json` (type, weapon, health, clip from `Data:HeroData.json`; release year from
`Data:HeroReleases.json`; pronouns from hero infoboxes; ability names; English "Select" voice lines) and downloads
splash art (`img/splash`), weapon renders and names (`img/weapon`), hero portraits (`img/hero`), ability icons (`img/ability`) and voice lines (`audio`). It keeps the hand-written `emoji`
and `added` fields, skips files already downloaded, and prints a TODO list of anything the wiki doesn't have yet.

Adding a hero after launch: run the script, write its `emoji`, and give it `"added": "YYYY-MM-DD"` (today or later,
never earlier) so past days keep their answers. Only add it once it has art, icons and voice lines. Never change
`LAUNCH` or a mode's `salt` in `app.js` after launch.

## License & credits

- Code: [MIT](LICENSE).
- `heroes.json`: data from [deadlock.wiki](https://deadlock.wiki) contributors, [CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/).
- `img/` and `audio/`: art, icons and voice lines © Valve Corporation, not covered by this repo's license.

Fan project, not affiliated with or endorsed by Valve. Deadlock is a trademark of Valve Corporation.

Yash-Singh1/wipeout-xl-rewrite.readme:
# Wipeout XL / 2097

This project is a rewrite of Wipeout XL / 2097 inspired by [wipeout-rewrite](https://github.com/phoboslab/wipeout-rewrite). It is based off a decompilation of the PS1 version of Wipeout XL & 2097 and another partial decompilation of the PC release.

The goal of this project is to keep the original behavior as much as possible while also upgrading the game with more capabilities. Here is a rough list of the changes in this game compared with the original PS1 version:
- Higher resolutions (HD Mod support, accurate rendering w/out PGXP)
- Uncapped framerates (physics & game logic still limited to original framerate)
- Widescreen support
- Split-screen for one on one mode
- Loading in Wipeout and Wipeout 64 tracks (this won't be perfect but it works pretty well right now)
- Higher render distance (configurable if you prefer older style)
- Custom music
- Touch controls for mobile and web (WIP)
- Autosave & converting save files
- Minor culling & depth buffer fixes

If you would like to change any of the settings or files for the game press the <kbd>`</kbd> or <kbd>~</kbd> key on your keyboard to toggle the debug UI. It has multiple tabs with many options to configure.

## Getting Started

To play this game, you will need a copy of Wipeout XL or Wipeout 2097. Store it somewhere on your computer.

If you are on Windows & macOS, you can download the latest build from the Releases and select your .cue file or archive of your PS1 rom when the app or exe prompts you for your game files. Users on all other platforms will have to [build](#build) the launcher themselves.

## SLOP LINE - Everything below this line is autogenerated

The PlayStation game (USA, SCUS-94351) running natively on macOS, Linux and
Windows, and in a web browser. One code base builds all four (the same game, the
same platform layer over SDL3 and OpenGL; the web uses WebGL 2). The game is the console's own code: the decompiled C of the retail
executable, compiled for the PC, with the PlayStation libraries replaced by the
platform layer (OpenGL drawing at any resolution, the sound chip, the CD drive,
pads and memory cards). It plays like the console, frame for frame: see
[docs/LOCKSTEP.md](docs/LOCKSTEP.md) for the comparison with recordings of the
real game.

## What you need

- Your copy of the PlayStation disc (Wipeout XL USA, or WipEout 2097 Europe):
  a `.cue` with its `.bin` tracks, a `.bin` without its `.cue`, or an archive
  of either (`.7z`, `.zip`, `.rar`, `.tar`, `.gz` and the like). The music
  plays from the disc's audio tracks, the intro and ending movies from its
  movie files.
- To build: CMake, Ninja, a C compiler (Clang or GCC), and SDL3 3.2 or later
  (zlib for the test traces is optional). Where CMake does not find SDL3 it
  downloads and builds it (`-DWIPEOUT_BUILD_SDL=ON` always does). The same
  goes for libarchive (`libarchive-dev` on Linux, Homebrew's `libarchive` on
  macOS; `-DWIPEOUT_BUILD_LIBARCHIVE=ON` always builds it).

## Build

Each build has its own folder under `build/`. macOS (Homebrew's `sdl3`):

```sh
cmake -S . -B build/mac -G Ninja -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=RelWithDebInfo
ninja -C build/mac
```

It also makes `build/mac/Wipeout XL.app`, with the Mac version's icon and the
Homebrew libraries it uses inside (copy it to `/Applications`).

Linux (for example Debian 13 or Ubuntu 25.04: `libsdl3-dev libgl-dev`): the
same two commands with `build/linux`.

Windows, with MSYS2's MinGW-w64 (UCRT64 or CLANG64 shell, packages `cmake`
`ninja` `gcc` or `clang`): the same two commands with `build/windows`. From
macOS or Linux, with the MinGW-w64 cross compiler, use the toolchain file:

```sh
cmake -S . -B build/windows -G Ninja -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release \
      -DCMAKE_TOOLCHAIN_FILE=cmake/mingw-w64-x86_64.cmake
ninja -C build/windows
```

`wipeoutxl.exe` is a single file, with SDL3 and the C runtime linked in and the
PC version's icon.

The web, with Emscripten:

```sh
emcmake cmake -S . -B build/web -G Ninja -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release \
      -DWIPEOUT_WEB_DISC="path/to/Wipeout XL (USA).cue"
ninja -C build/web
```

This makes `wipeoutxl.html`, `wipeoutxl.js` and `wipeoutxl.wasm`, and, as
wipeout-rewrite's web build has its data beside the page, the disc the page
loads by itself: `WIPEOUT_WEB_DISC` (your own copy) links the `.cue` and its
`.bin` tracks into `build/web/disc/` and writes `wipeoutxl-data.json`, which
names it. Put `build/web` on any web server with the links followed
(`cp -RL build/web site`), or try it with `python3 -m http.server` in
`build/web` and open `http://localhost:8000/wipeoutxl.html`. A host can also
put a disc there by hand: `disc/Wipeout XL (USA).cue` with its tracks is found
without a `wipeoutxl-data.json`, and the JSON (`{ "disc": "url/of/the.cue" }`)
can point anywhere on the site. With `-DWIPEOUT_WEB_DISC_MUSIC=OFF` only the
data track goes into `disc/` (about 86 MB in place of about 700): the game
plays, without its music.

## Phones and tablets (iOS, Android)

The same game runs on iPhone, iPad and Android, landscape and full screen (OpenGL ES 3), with touch controls
(below) and widescreen on from the start. SDL3 and libarchive are downloaded and built into the app.

iOS (Xcode; the simulator needs no signing):

```sh
cmake -S . -B build/ios -G Ninja -DCMAKE_SYSTEM_NAME=iOS -DCMAKE_OSX_SYSROOT=iphonesimulator \
      -DCMAKE_OSX_ARCHITECTURES=arm64 -DCMAKE_OSX_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET=15.0 -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=RelWithDebInfo
ninja -C build/ios wipeoutxl
codesign --force --sign - "build/ios/Wipeout XL.app"
xcrun simctl install booted "build/ios/Wipeout XL.app"
```

For a device, configure with `-G Xcode -DCMAKE_SYSTEM_NAME=iOS -DWIPEOUT_IOS_TEAM=<your team id>
-DWIPEOUT_IOS_BUNDLE_ID=<an id of yours>`, open the project in Xcode and run it on the device (the first
configure takes a while: Xcode checks every one of libarchive's tests). Put the disc image (the `.cue` with its
`.bin` files, or a `.zip`/`.7z` of them) in the Files app, On My iPhone (or iPad) > Wipeout XL;

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Faster pictures: fewer GPU batches and passes, less idle time

Measured in a race (widescreen, a 1600x1000 window, pictures between frames
uncapped), at 5x render scale from about 110 to about 180 pictures a second
(runs vary with what else uses the GPU):

- One premultiplied blend for every blending but the console's subtraction:
  the shader writes how much of what is behind stays, so semi-transparent,
  faded and glyph primitives share batches, and a textured semi-transparent
  primitive is no longer a batch (two draws) of its own. Opaque ones are drawn
  without blending. The pictures are the same, pixel for pixel, as before.
- The depth buffer's second (depth-writing) pass is left out for batches that
  cannot write it (2D, the sky, faded or untextured semi-transparent ones): it
  ran the whole fragment shader over the screen's clears and backdrops.
- The CD drive's first response to a command is sped up as its reads are: the
  race's CD position query each frame waited 1.5 ms of the console's time.
- The pacing draws another picture when half of one still fits before the
  game's next field (it slept out the rest of the field).

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Depth buffer: a polygon seen from behind is hidden by anything nearer

With the menus' track models drawn two-sided, their backs showed through
their fronts in bands (the domes of Talon's Reach): the depth test's slack,
there to keep decals in the game's order, let a back face drawn after the
front at nearly its depth win; and a batch's depth is written only when it
is drawn, so a back face in the same batch as the front never met it. A

The per-pixel depth test (off by default) is gone with its depth buffers, the sky's mark that kept it from
the sky (PortBackground, GteSetBackground) and WIPEOUT_DEPTH. Near polygons over the console GPU's size

Debug console sized to the game window

The console was scaled by the display's density on top of the backend's own (twice the size on a Retina
display) and so overflowed smaller windows. Its layout, made for 720 points across, is now scaled every
frame to fit the window (at most 92% of its width, 90% of its height), and it is centred when it opens.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Uncapped frame rate: pictures between the game's 30 frames a second

The game keeps its 30 frames a second; the display draws as often as the settings allow (uncapped by
default, VSync, a cap, or the console's 60 fields). Swap tells the platform which ordering tables it will
draw once its fields have passed (PsxUpcomingTables); while it waits, those tables are drawn again and
again with every projected vertex placed between its view-space positions in the frame before and this
one by the time passed.

The renderers key what they project (gte.h): a model's vertex and which drawing of the model it is (the
ships by their number), a track vertex, a grid point by its face and place, a particle, a near-clipped
point by its edge, and libgte's persistent vertices by their address. What one frame has and the other
not (track coming into view) moves with the view's motion, fitted to the vertices both frames share; a
camera cut is not interpolated. The redraws touch neither the CPU's copy of video memory, nor the traces,
nor the frame recorder.

Batches now split only on blending and depth state (texture page, palette, window and colour depth go with
each vertex): about 140 draw calls a frame instead of about 1950, pixel for pixel the same pictures. The
lockstep result on the arcade recording is unchanged. WIPEOUT_INTERPOLATE=n draws n pictures a field in
fixed-step test runs.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Widescreen: a race fills a wider window, the HUD at its edges

With the setting on (Graphics tab, widescreen = 1, WIPEOUT_WIDESCREEN=1) the screen's columns of video
memory are drawn into a framebuffer that reaches past both sides by as much as the window's shape asks;
the game's projections past the screen's edges are drawn there, and untextured fills and fades across
the screen stretch over the sides. Video memory's copy is brought up to date before anything reads it,
and CPU writes go to both. Only a race's scene is shown wide (the game says so each frame it draws one):
menus, loading screens, movies and the split window stay 4:3.

The HUD's packets are grouped into elements (packets that touch); an element wholly on the left or right
goes to that edge, what reaches the middle stays. The far view's screen tests take in the sides. With the
setting off nothing changes: the lockstep result on the arcade recording is the same as before.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

The Windows release's key caps, and the disc's own movies

Keyboard glyphs: ESC, ENTER and the gold arrows are the Windows release's HUD2 art, texel for
texel (platform/keyglyphs.c, made by tools/gen_keyglyphs.py), drawn at that release's size. The
keys it has no cap for (SPACE, ALT, S, F1, A, D) get caps made of the same pieces: the cap's face,
letters drawn as the ESC legend's, and the legend's engraved rim.

Movies: the intro and endings play from the PS1 disc's MAKE.AV and XTRO1-4.AV, as the console's
player streams them: MDEC frames (version 1/2 bitstream) decoded per sector arrival at double
speed, XA ADPCM sound (bit-exact with ffmpeg's decoder). The PC release's MPEGs, pl_mpeg and the
--pc-data option are gone: the PS1 disc is all the port needs. Fixed-step runs still skip the
movies unless WIPEOUT_MOVIES is set, so the tests' capture numbers stay as they were.

No black flicker at the far view's nearest depths or beside near walls; Tab and a magnifier for the frame recorder

The far view's depth table lost everything sorted into its first bucket (depth 32760-32792): that
bucket is the table's tail, whose link PortFarDraw rewrites to join the game's table. Track faces
and objects crossing that depth, where the game's drawing hands over to the far view, vanished for a
frame and the black backdrop showed through. Bucket 0 is no longer used.

Scenery polygons the game leaves out for a vertex too near the camera, behind it or beyond the GPU's
coordinates (a wall the ship passes close by) are clipped at the near plane and drawn, in the game's
own pass: corners the game projected keep their exact positions, so they meet their neighbours.

The frame recorder freezes on Tab instead of F9 (F9 is Select again, as documented); the Frames tab
shows a magnifier of the pixels under the pointer, and draws the recorded pictures with sharp pixels.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Frame recorder (F9) and no flickering far walls in the tunnels

Frame recorder (platform/psx/framecap.c): the last three seconds of
drawing are kept: every primitive as libgpu drew it (corners with their
precise positions and depths, colours, texture, blending, whether the
GPU's size limit skipped it), what game code built it (PortTagPrims in
objdraw, trackdraw, object.c's environment maps, the screen clear), the
video memory it was textured from and the picture shown. F9 freezes the
game and saves them; the debug console's Frames tab steps back through
the frames and lists every primitive at a clicked pixel with the colour
it writes there. tools/framecap.py reads the saved frames (pixel,
prim, flicker). Setting record_frames, on by default.

The tunnels' black specks: the game culls a polygon that faces away
judging on its corners rounded to whole pixels. A far wall polygon a
few pixels across, nearly edge on, came out facing away in one frame and
not in the next; the far view took the game's word and left it out too,
so the black backdrop at the end of the tunnel showed through for a
frame. Such polygons are now judged again on the precise positions, and
left to the far view when they face the camera. In a recorded climb on
Talon's Reach the object primitives that vanished for a single frame
went from 257 to 116; what remains is ship models turning, polygons
under a pixel and the pickup effect, as on the console.

Also: the replay recorder (--record, record_replays, off by default).

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

No black holes in the track beside the camera

A track face right beside the camera has a corner far off the screen or
too near the lens. The console then loses it twice over: the game drops
every cell with such a corner, and the GPU skips any triangle wider than
1023 or taller than 511 pixels. For a frame or two there was a hole in
the track just in front of the ship, showing the black background.

- libgpu draws a triangle over the GPU's size limit when every corner is
  a projection it knows in 3D (setting large_polygons, on by default;
  WIPEOUT_LARGE_POLYGONS=0 restores the console's rule).
- The far view no longer leaves out faces with such corners: it clips
  them at a near plane in camera space and draws the visible part as
  triangles, behind what the game drew of the face.

Debug console on the backtick key, with saved settings

Dear ImGui 1.92.9b (MIT, platform/third_party/imgui, with its SDL3 and
OpenGL 3 backends) draws a console over the game: frame rates (display and
game) with a frame-time graph and an on-screen overlay; the draw distance
(console / whole track), the fade and its range, the depth test, full
screen; skipping the intro movie; the settings file and the memory cards'
folder, with a field to move the saves (at the next start). The settings
live in wipeoutxl.ini in the user's data folder (platform/settings.c),
saved as they change and applied live; environment variables still
override them, and the tests' hidden runs ignore the file. While the
console is open it has the keyboard and mouse (key releases still reach the
game). WIPEOUT_DEBUG_UI=<tab> opens it in a hidden test run.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Depth buffer off by default: decals no longer fight their surfaces

The game's models carry decals on or just in front of the surfaces behind
them (sign faces on their boards, the FSOL screen's picture, the flat
pieces of the menus' spinning track models and medals) and rely on the
drawing order. With the per-pixel depth test those surfaces z-fought:
pieces flickered in and out as the models turned, and the F sign was cut
by its own board. The vanishing band that looked like a depth problem was
the far view's (00cb541). Polygons are drawn in the console's order again;
WIPEOUT_DEPTH=1 brings the depth test back.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Far view: no band where scenery vanishes ahead of the player

The GTE rejects a polygon with any vertex deeper than 32767 (IR3
saturates), but the game draws scenery objects to 38200: objects in
between were drawn by the game with nothing coming out, and the far view
skipped them as drawn. On screen, a band at a fixed distance ahead in
which everything disappeared and came back. The object renderer now
records each primitive it drew or culled; the far view draws the rest of
any object. Track faces count as drawn only when all their medium or high
detail cells came out; partly drawn ones are drawn whole by the far view a
hair deeper, behind the game's cells. About 5 objects a frame on
Sagarmatha were affected.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

WIPEOUT_NO_GAMEPAD starts without touching the controllers

SDL's controller start opens every HID device; when the system's game
controller service hangs (gamecontrollerd stuck, as it was), that open never
returns and the game freezes before its window appears, beyond Ctrl+C.
With WIPEOUT_NO_GAMEPAD the controller subsystem is not started at all
(unless a test script attaches virtual pads), so the game still starts and
plays with the keyboard.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

The window's picture is opaque: no black holes where shadows are

The subtractive blend the ship shadows use (and the distance fade's) also
blended the framebuffer's alpha, down to 0 under every shadow. The window
system composites the window with that alpha, so on screen each shadow was
a see-through hole showing black: under the rivals ahead it moved along the
track in front of the player. Captures read only RGB and never showed it.
The window's alpha is now set to 1 before each frame is shown;
WIPEOUT_ALPHA_CHECK counts see-through pixels in captured frames (0 now, in
a full Sagarmatha race).

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

A depth buffer: 3D polygons hide each other per pixel

The console drew polygons in the ordering table's order, each one sorted by
its average depth, so large or intersecting ones poked through what was in
front of them and parts of meshes came and went as they turned. The
renderer now has a depth buffer: every primitive with precise projections
is depth tested (perspective depth from the projections' view z), opaque
texels write it, semi-transparent and faded ones only test it. 2D
primitives (HUD, fills, sprites built in 2D) and the sky (projected while
PortBackground is on) are drawn as before, in the table's order. The
buffer is cleared for each ordering table. WIPEOUT_DEPTH=0 turns it off.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Far view: the track faces the game dropped are drawn too

The far view skipped every section the game's renderers had walked, but
the game drops a face of a listed section when a corner is more than 16
bits from the camera or beyond the GTE's depth range. Those faces were
drawn by nobody: a black hole at the end of the visible track that kept
ahead of the player (under the FEED ME sign at the start of Talon's
Reach). The renderers now mark the faces they draw, and the far view draws
every other face in sight.

derekboy15/recruit-plus.readme:
# Recruit+ (Warhammer 40,000 9th Edition)

A learn-to-play army builder and game companion for 40k 9th Edition. Unofficial fan-made tool, not affiliated with Games Workshop.

- Design: `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-10-20-recruit-plus-design.md`
- Packages: `packages/data` (data pipeline), `apps/web` (PWA)

```bash
npm install
npm run data:fetch   # downloads BSData wh40k-9e v9.8.0 (sha256-verified)
npm run data:build   # writes packages/data/generated/
npm test
npm run dev
```

More checks: `npm run typecheck`, `npm run build` then `npm run budgets -w apps/web` (size budgets, `docs/perf.md`), and `npm run e2e` (the dev-server flows, then the production build with its service worker: offline, accessibility, phone performance, installability).

To publish the site (Supabase, GitHub, Vercel), follow `DEPLOY.md`.

artificialfear/grudgeball.readme:
# Grudge Ball

A team review game for band class, made to run on a classroom viewboard with a mini basketball hoop.

**Play it:** https://artificialfear.github.io/grudgeball/

## How the game works
- Teams start with 8 hearts (max 12). On their turn, a team picks a mystery box.
- **Question:** the team has 15 seconds. If they get it right, they take a heart from another team, then one player shoots until they miss. Each basket is +1 heart for their team or one more heart taken from another team.
- **Wrong answer:** the team loses a heart. Then the other teams get a chance to steal, one at a time in turn order. Each team has 5 seconds to choose steal or pass; running out of time counts as a pass. A team that steals gets a fresh 5 seconds to answer. A wrong steal costs a heart. A correct steal takes a heart from another team but gets no shots, and turn order doesn't change.
- **Gang-up rule:** if one team attacks a team and a different team attacks it on the very next turn, the attacked team gets a bonus turn right away. Steal attacks don't count toward this.
- **Sudden death (0 hearts):** the team can't attack. A correct answer earns 1 heart back, with no shots. A wrong answer means the team is out.
- **Items:** a team can hold 2 items and play only one per turn. Finding a third means throwing one away.
  - **Shield**: no one can attack you until your next turn.
  - **Lifesteal Ring**: for the rest of this turn, every heart you take heals you +1.
  - **Cursed Sword**: for two of your turns, your attacks take 2 hearts, but attacks on you also take 2.
  - **Reed of Resurrection**: if your team is knocked out, it comes back with 2 hearts automatically.
  - **Metronome**: +10 seconds on your question.
  - **Repeat Sign** 𝄇: your team goes again right after this turn.
  - **Fermata**: pick a team; it can't steal on the next wrong answer.
  - **Modulation**: reverses the turn order (only one per game).
  - **Three Free Shots** (used right away): three shots no matter what.
  - **Traumatic Scale** (used right away): lose a heart.
- **Final round** 🏁: tap it when class is almost over. Choose "finish this round" or "one more full round". Every team still in ends with the same number of turns (bonus turns still play), then the winner screen shows.
- **Fairness:**
  - **Shooters rotate:** students number off, and the game calls who shoots next.
  - **Underdog bonus:** the last-place team gets +1 heart whenever it opens an item box.
  - **Leader tax:** a team at max hearts can't collect items.

- **Action animations:** hits fly from the attacking team to its target ("HIT BY RED"), and the Shield, Ring, Sword, Reed, Metronome, Repeat Sign, Fermata, Modulation, lifesteal, sudden death and knockouts each have a short effect on the team cards. They can be turned off on the setup screen.

All of these can be adjusted on the setup screen.

## Editing questions
Use **Edit questions** in the game itself. Write one question per line as `Question | Answer`, or keep your questions in a Google Sheet (column A = question, column B = answer) and paste the columns in. The header row, blank rows and any extra columns are skipped.
Question sets save in that browser. Use **Export .txt** to back them up or move them to another device.

## Music questions (made fresh every game)
Besides the written questions, each game adds new **listening** 🎧 and **staff** 🎼 questions (3 of each by default, set on the setup screen). The level follows the question set's name ("Level 3 …" makes Level 3 questions) or can be picked by hand.
- **Listening:** tap ▶ Play. The question clock starts when the sound ends; replaying restarts it, so stealing teams can hear it again too. Level 1: higher/lower, same/different, up/down, fast/slow. Level 2: major/minor chords, steps/skips, crescendo/decrescendo, meter in 3 or 4, staccato/legato. Level 3: major/minor scales, 2nd/3rd/5th/octave, accelerando/ritardando. Level 4: interval quality, major/minor/diminished chords, chromatic scale.
- **Staff:** notation is drawn on screen. Level 1: note names on the staff, note and rest values. Level 2: ledger lines and accidentals, adding up beats, counting sharps/flats. Level 3: naming major keys, interval numbers, sixteenth-note rhythms. Level 4: interval quality, major/minor triads, relative minors.
- The answer key (☰ menu) shows every music question with its staff or a play button.
- **Test speakers** on the setup screen plays a short chord.

## Built-in question sets
The `questions/` folder holds the sets that come with the game and show up in the Questions dropdown on every device:
- Level 1 Beginner: Rank 3 vocab, note values, staff and clefs, piano landmarks, instruments
- Level 2 Developing: Ranks 4–5 vocab, eighth notes, dotted notes, ties, repeats, key signatures, partials
- Level 3 Intermediate: Ranks 6–7 vocab, sixteenths, triplets, 6/8, syncopation, scales, enharmonics
- Level 4 Advanced: Ranks 8–10 vocab, key signatures, transposition, chords, intervals, compound meter

Each file is one set: a `# Set: Name` line, then `Question | Answer` lines. Run `python3 build.py` after editing.

## Files
- `index.html`: the game, with all art built in. This is the file GitHub Pages serves.
- `src/grudgeball.src.html`: the editable source, with image placeholders.
- `assets/`: the art taken from the original myViewBoard file.
- `sounds/`: the game's sound effects and menu music, as MP3s. To change a sound, upload a new MP3 with the **same file name** (for example `sounds/correct.mp3`). basketball.mp3 plays when the Free Shots box opens, open-box.mp3 when any mystery box opens, make-basket.mp3 on MADE IT, final-round.mp3 when a final round is started and again when its last turn begins, victory.mp3 on the winner screen, select.mp3 on ordinary button taps, and attack.mp3 when a team is hit (timed so its impact lands when the attack animation strikes the card). Sounds without a file (Fermata, Modulation) use built-in beeps.
- `src/music.js`: makes the listenin

# Galaga - native SDL2 port (work in progress)

A C11 / SDL2 port of the 1981 Namco arcade game for Linux handhelds
(PortMaster: ArkOS, ROCKNIX, muOS, Knulli), desktops (Linux, Windows, macOS) and the
web, checked against the original ROM running in MAME.

**Status:** the game runs in C, equal frame for frame (pictures and sound)
to an emulated Galaga board that is itself checked against MAME, with the
DIP switches (`galaga.cfg` and an operator menu), the high scores kept
(`galaga.hiscore`) and the cocktail table's flip. Next: testing on devices
and a release. See
[GALAGA_PORT_PLAN.md](GALAGA_PORT_PLAN.md).

You need your own MAME `galaga` ROM set (`galaga.zip`); none is included.
The first run extracts what the game needs from it to `assets/` next to
the program. The emulated board (`--emulate`) and the MAME tests also need
the device ROMs `namco51.zip` and `namco54.zip` next to it.

Converted by monkeyx.

```bash
cmake -S . -B build && cmake --build build -j
build/galaga --windowed --rom /path/to/galaga.zip
```

## Controls

One control panel, as on the upright cabinet: the players take turns, and
every connected pad drives the panel.

| Action | Pad | Keyboard |
|---|---|---|
| Left / right | left stick or D-pad | Left Right |
| Fire | A or B | Space or Ctrl |
| Coin | Select | 5 |
| 1-player start | Start | 1 or Enter |
| 2-player start | L1 + Start | 2 |
| Next graphics preset | Select + L1 | F3 |
| Glow on / off | | F4 |
| CRT scanlines on / off | | F5 |
| Operator menu (DIP switches) | Select + R1 | F2 |
| Quit | hold Select + Start for 1 s | Esc |

## Building

Needs CMake 3.13+, a C11 compiler and SDL 2.0.10+.

```bash
ctest --test-dir build              # tests (ROM and MAME tests need roms/galaga.zip, namco51.zip, namco54.zip and mame)
cmake --build build --target package_linux package_portmaster
emcmake cmake -S . -B build-web && cmake --build build-web --target serve
```

## License

Apache 2.0 for the source; see [NOTICE](NOTICE) for the third-party material
this project refers to. No ROM data is included or distributed.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

The main loop as Galaxian's: no step due, sleep to the next

Nothing is drawn or presented between the game's frames; the loop sleeps
until the next one is due (vsync or not), as Galaxian's does. The fresh
flag of video_present goes again. The plan notes the scalers carried to
the sibling ports.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Less CPU per frame: draw once a tick, cheaper scalers

- main.c draws only when the game stepped; video_present uploads the
  texture only for a new frame, and the loop waits 1 ms when presenting
  returns at once (no vsync) instead of spinning
- gfx/scale.c: neighbours read without bounds checks inside the picture,
  flat xBR pixels written at once, and no premultiply / unpremultiply of
  an opaque clamped picture (the game's frame): the same output bit for
  bit (game frames at 2x, 3x, 4x, both scalers; test enhance), 4x crisp
  3.3 -> 2.7 ms, smooth 4.5 -> 3.8 ms a frame

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

C3: the game in C is the default, its sound equal to the board's

- sim.c makes the frame's sound as the board does: the WSG's writes and
  the 54xx's O port at their samples in the frame, through emu/wsg.c and
  emu/noise54.c; frame now compares every frame's samples too (equal

  (the difference overflowed after 10 s; UBSan)

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

C0: the five programs whole in C on the board's scheduler; frame equal through a game

The C game is now each CPU's program ported whole, every instruction a
case of one resumable function: main, sub and sub2 (sim/*_run.c) and the
51xx's and 54xx's MB88 programs (m51_run.c, m54_run.c), run by sim.c as
the board runs its CPUs (attosecond time, slices, syncs, timers, the
06xx and its select lines, the 51xx's timer from the vertical blank).

What made it equal to the board frame for frame:
- a Z80 stops between machine cycles at every access the board's does:
  the fetches after an instruction's first byte (measured on emu/z80.c),
  data accesses, an interrupt's pushes; LD (nn),rr through those too
- the MCUs scheduled as CPUs: their whole instructions end slices short
  and so set where the Z80s' slices end
- F whole (P/V, bits 3 and 5, Q for SCF/CCF, WZ for BIT n,(HL), the
  block repeats), as an interrupt's PUSH AF stores it
- the IRQ held one instruction after EI, taken after RETN; the registers
  at reset as the board's (F $40, IX and IY $FFFF)

The routine-by-routine ports, their checker (test_sim) and the
functional 51xx (io.c, test_io) are gone: test_mcu checks the MCU
programs step for step against emu/mb88.c, and frame (now in ctest)
checks the whole C game against the board from power-on through a game.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

C0: main's foreground in C, counting cycles; a frame of the C game

main's IRQ, tasks and subroutines are generated again (with the hand
edits) counting Z80 cycles as the board's Z80 takes them (checked over
2506 instruction addresses); its foreground from $02D3 is one resumable
function, every instruction a place to go on from, which stops at the
vertical blank by its cycles, as the board's would. sim.c runs a frame:
the 51xx's loop, the two IRQs in the order the board interleaves them,
the foreground, sub2's NMIs; the 06xx's transfers happen at once with
their NMIs' cycles. test_frame hands the C game the board's state and
compares them frame by frame (not yet a test: the IRQs' handshakes and
races need a scheduler for the three programs).

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

C0: the 51xx in C, checked against the board's

sim/io.c ports the 51xx's MB8843 program: its once-a-frame loop line by
line (translated, then read), its interrupt's commands and the buffer it
hands out a byte per select rise; io_transfer stands in for the 06xx.
test_io follows main's transfers on the board and checks every byte main
reads from the board's 51xx against the C one, with the default switches
and five other coinages (257097 bytes, all equal).

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

C0: main's IRQ and its tasks in C; the checker leaner

main's IRQ and its 24 tasks, with the subroutines they call, line by line
on sim/cpu.h (drafted by a translator kept out of the repository, then
read): the attract mode's script and its demo, the attacks, the formation,
the stars, the credits, the bombs and the rest. LD A,R goes through
game_r, which the checker feeds the board's values; the waits on another
CPU go through game_wait_for. The extractor writes the three programs'
bytes whole (past their tables they read code as data too). test_sim
tracks writes as lists rather than copying memory at each call (40 s,
from 89), and can write the PCs its run reaches for the listings.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

C0: a player for the checker's run; flags for DAA in the line-by-line ports

test_sim plays an attract cycle, then games one after another (one and
two players by turns) with a player that aims at the nearest enemy and
moves away from what is about to reach the ship's row, powering the board
on again after each game. Races are now caught on addresses the CPU had
already written. cpu.h keeps H and N for DAA and has the divide and
multiply main and sub share. The plan notes where MAME's 51xx sees its
select line late: its MB88s start a Z80 cycle before its Z80s.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

C0: sub's IRQ in C: the sprite banks, the motion scripts, shots and hits

Ported line by line where the code carries registers and flags between
blocks (sim/cpu.h). The checker treats a CPU's wait on another's
handshake as such, checks the IRQ from its vector, and fails if a
routine reads ROM bytes outside the extracted tables; the extractor
writes sub's scripts and tables.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

C0: the C game's state and a routine checker for three CPUs; sub2's sound driver in C

sim/game.c keeps the board's memory as the ROMs lay it out; sim/sound.c is
sub2's NMI and sound driver, equal to the ROM's at every one of 58568 calls
in a 30000-frame scripted run (test sim). Its tables join tables.txt.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

X1: the extractor: tiles, sprites, palette and lookups, font, waveforms, tables, previews

galaga --extract writes them from the player's ROM set (development builds
after each build); gfx/galaga.c reads them back. extract: byte-identical runs,
everything read back is the set's, the font reads the board's title screen.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

E2: the Namco WSG and the 54xx's noise, modelled from MAME's output

The WSG's three voices from the waveform PROM, (sample - 8) x volume x 48;
the 54xx's two O-port levels through band-passes at 182 and 517 Hz fitted to
MAME's output with the WSG muted. mame_emu: 554 of 555 1/10 s windows of the
scripted run within 3 dB of MAME's recording. The program streams the sound.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

E1: three Z80s, the MB88xx core, the Galaga board on MAME's scheduler, video and starfield, checked against MAME

The board runs main, sub, sub2 and the 51xx/54xx MCUs in MAME's slices
(attosecond time, its divisor, syncs, Z80s stopping between machine cycles)
and equals MAME's traces instruction for instruction over 100 frames of play
(the 51xx's read-mode select timing aside), and its memory and pictures,
stars included, at 15 frames from power-on through a minute of play.

nicholaspanico97-art/Islandwar.readme:
# Island War

A multiplayer team game: two islands, two teams. Gather, build an industrial base, research, and
attack across the water with player-piloted planes, missiles and ships. Win by delivering a nuke
to the enemy's industrial core. Think old modded Minecraft military sandbox, arcade not simulation.

The full design and build order are in [docs/game-plan.md](docs/game-plan.md). Decisions are logged
in [docs/decisions.md](docs/decisions.md), and [docs/testing.md](docs/testing.md) has the exact
commands to test each milestone.

**Status:** M0 (project skeleton). Not yet launched in the engine; see "Versions" below.

## Versions

| Tool | Version | Status |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Godot | 4.7.2-stable, .NET build | Chosen. C# compiles against `Godot.NET.Sdk/4.7.2`; the engine itself hasn't been run yet. |
| .NET SDK | 8.0 (`net8.0`) | Verified: builds and tests pass with 8.0.132. |
| Physics | Jolt (built into Godot) | Enabled in `project.godot`. |
| godot_voxel | v1.7 is the latest release | Pending the M0 test; a custom C# mesher is the fallback. |
| xUnit | 2.9.2 | Sim unit tests. |

## Quick start

```sh
./build.sh test                                # Sim unit tests, no engine needed
./build.sh server --port=7777                  # headless dedicated server
./build.sh client --connect=127.0.0.1:7777     # a client, in another terminal
```

On Windows use `.\build.ps1` with the same arguments. Engine commands need Godot 4.7.2 (.NET) on `PATH`
as `godot`, or the `GODOT` environment variable pointing at it.

## Layout

```
project.godot, Main.tscn, Main.cs   Godot project and entry scene (picks server or client)
IslandWar.csproj                    Godot C# assembly: Client/, Server/, Net/
Client/                             rendering, input, UI
Server/                             dedicated server entry, match orchestration
Net/                                replication (from M1b)
Sim/                                game rules: plain C#, no Godot dependency
tests/IslandWar.Sim.Tests/          xUnit tests for Sim
data/                               tunables (JSON); never hardcode these
docs/                               plan, decisions, testing
```

Game rules go in `Sim/`, which can't reference Godot, so they stay unit-testable without a renderer.

TanakritEuro/voxel-sandbox.readme:
# Voxel Sandbox

A Minecraft-like voxel sandbox for the browser, built with Three.js and TypeScript.

```bash
npm install
npm run dev
```

Open http://localhost:5173 and click to play.

| Input | Action |
| --- | --- |
| Mouse | Look |
| W A S D | Walk (or fly) |
| Space | Jump; in water: swim up; flying: up |
| Shift | Crouch (won't walk off edges); flying: down |
| Ctrl (tap) | Sprint until you stop moving forward; flying: faster |
| F, or Space twice | Start or stop flying |
| Left button (hold) | Break block (stone takes longest) |
| Right click | Place block |
| 1–9 or wheel | Pick a block |
| Esc | Release the mouse |

Add `?seed=123` to the URL for a different world, `?at=x,z` to start somewhere else (with
the default seed: desert `?at=384,0`, snowy mountains `?at=0,192`, forest `?at=-121,-226`).

Measuring: `?stats` shows the performance overlay (F3 toggles it), `?autofly` flies a fixed
path at sprint speed for 30 s and prints a frame-time report, `?radius=12` sets the view
radius (8 by default), `?workers=1` the number of chunk workers. `npm run bench` times

youssefmmalak/chess.readme:
# Chess Academy

A personal chess academy: a structured path from complete beginner toward strong, competitive play.
Interactive lessons you play through on the board, tactics that adapt to you, a computer opponent,
engine-powered game review with plain-language coaching, an opening repertoire, endgame drills,
spaced repetition and an honest progress system.

Everything runs in the browser. There is no account and no server; progress is stored on the device.

## Quick start

```bash
npm install          # also needed once for the Stockfish engine files
npm run dev          # http://localhost:5173
```

Production build (static files in `dist/`, deployable to any static host; installable as a PWA):

```bash
npm run build
npm run preview      # http://localhost:4173
```

Requirements: Node 20+ and a modern browser (WebAssembly + Web Workers; Safari 16+, Chrome, Firefox, Edge).

## Deploying (Vercel)

`vercel.json` holds the whole configuration (Vite, `npm ci`, `npm run build`, output `dist`,
cache headers for the PWA and the Stockfish WASM). No environment variables are needed.

1. Import the GitHub repository at https://vercel.com/new and keep the detected settings.
2. Vercel deploys the repository's default branch to production and every later push automatically.
3. To test a live deployment from a machine that can reach it:
   `E2E_BASE_URL=https://<your-app>.vercel.app PLAYWRIGHT_CHROMIUM=/path/to/chrome npm run test:e2e`

**iPhone:** open the URL in Safari → Share → Add to Home Screen. Progress is stored on the device,
and the Home Screen app's storage is separate from Safari's; use Settings → Export/Restore backup
to move progress between them or to another device.

## What is in the app

| Area | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Home** | The next lesson and today’s plan: built from your time budget, stage, due reviews, puzzle accuracy, weakest theme and unreviewed games. Every item says *why* it is there. |
| **Learn** | 8 levels, 52 lessons. Each has explanations, demonstrations, guided and practice exercises on a real board, and a mastery check you must pass. Level 1 lessons can be "tested out". Levels unlock by passing lessons, not by time. |
| **Practice** | Rated tactics near your level, spaced-repetition review, themed sets, and "Your mistakes": positions from your own analysed games. Graduated hints: where to look → the idea → which piece → full solution with the opponent’s best defence. |
| **Play** | Stockfish 19 (WebAssembly, in a Web Worker) at 8 levels; White/Black/random; practice mode (take-backs, hints) or serious mode; start from any FEN; games resume after a refresh. |
| **Analyze** | Engine review of your games or imported PGN (Chess.com/Lichess, clocks supported). Moves are classified best/strong/good/inaccuracy/mistake/blunder/book and missed opportunities are flagged. Mistakes get a seven-part explanation and become practice positions. Recurring patterns across games map to lessons. Explore variations, copy PGN/FEN, play on from any position. |
| **Openings** | A small repertoire (Italian Game, Alapin, French & Caro-Kann Advance, Scandinavian for White; 1…e5 and the QGD for Black): ideas, plans, mistakes, move-by-move explanations, recall drills with spaced repetition, traps, deviations, and a repertoire explorer. |
| **Endgames** | Drills against the engine’s best defence: queen/rook/two-bishop mates, king-and-pawn (opposition, square of the pawn), Lucena, Philidor. |
| **Progress** | Skill map with mastery levels, training minutes, puzzle rating trend, weekly accuracy, mistake rate in your games, results — with clear notes about what the numbers do and do not mean. |
| **Settings** | Daily time, goal, learning style, board theme, coordinates, legal-move hints, sound, motion, text size, backup export/import, reset. |

### How mastery works

`Not started → Learning → Practicing → Proficient → Mastered`. Opening a lesson only makes it
"Learning". Passing the mastery check makes it "Practicing". "Proficient" needs at least 80% clean
(unaided, first-try) recent answers across at least two days. "Mastered" needs at least 90% across
three or more days, including a successful review at least a week after first passing. The exact
rules are in `src/learning/mastery.ts`.

### Ratings: what they are and are not

- The **puzzle practice rating** is an Elo-style number for this app’s puzzles only. Only the
  first attempt at each puzzle counts; hints and wrong tries reduce credit, and two wrong tries
  earn nothing, so guessing does not pay. It is **not** comparable to Chess.com, Lichess or FIDE ratings.
- Computer **levels 1–4** are weakened by the app (candidate moves chosen with randomness) and are
  **not calibrated**. Levels 5–7 use Stockfish’s `UCI_Elo`, which Stockfish calibrates against
  engines rather than humans, and this app runs the smaller "lite" network — so treat those numbers
  as rough guides.
- The app does not estimate an official rating, and completing the curriculum does not guarantee any strength.

## Architecture

```
src/
  chess/      chess.js wrappers, PGN/FEN I/O, threat detection used by the coach
  board/      the interactive board (pointer + touch + keyboard, drag or click, promotion picker)
  engine/     UCI client, Stockfish service with automatic fallback, bots, game review, coach text
  content/    curriculum data: levels, lessons, puzzles, openings, endgame drills (see CONTENT_GUIDE.md)
  learning/   mastery, spaced repetition, puzzle rating, puzzle selection, daily plan, unlocks, patterns
  storage/    versioned schema, migrations, StorageAdapter (localStorage), store and pure actions
  exercises/  exercise renderers (move, collect, squares, choice, line)
  pages/      Home, Learn, LessonPlayer, Practice, Play, Analyze, Openings, Endgames, Progress, Settings
```

- **Rules:** all legality (king safety, castling, en passant, promotion, draws) comes from
  [chess.js](https://github.com/jhlywa/chess.js); nothing is re-implemented.
- **Engine:**

chrislanejones/future-chrislanejones-bea.readme:
# Chris Lane Jones — Beach Portfolio

A coastal home for my work, writing, and life beyond the browser. The 2026 beach version pairs Next.js, React and Convex with recorded St. Augustine Beach scenes and an interactive sandcastle.

[Portfolio](https://www.chrislanejones.com) · [Getting started](docs/chapters/01-getting-started/README.md) · [Change summary](docs/Change-summary.md)

![Beach portfolio homepage in light mode.](docs/images/beach-home-light.webp)

<details>
<summary>View dark mode</summary>

![Beach portfolio homepage in dark mode.](docs/images/beach-home-dark.webp)

</details>

## Read the book

Start at chapter 1 or open the area you are working on. Each chapter has its own README, source references, and links to the previous and next chapters.

| Chapter | Read more |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | [Getting started](docs/chapters/01-getting-started/README.md) |
| 2 | [Architecture and file map](docs/chapters/02-architecture/README.md) |
| 3 | [Pages and features](docs/chapters/03-features/README.md) |
| 4 | [Coastal design and scenes](docs/chapters/04-design-and-scenes/README.md) |
| 5 | [Content and media](docs/chapters/05-content-and-media/README.md) |
| 6 | [Authentication and security](docs/chapters/06-security/README.md) |
| 7 | [Search and metadata](docs/chapters/07-seo/README.md) |
| 8 | [Testing and dependencies](docs/chapters/08-maintenance/README.md) |
| 9 | [Deployment and operations](docs/chapters/09-deployment/README.md) |
| 10 | [Architecture decision records](docs/adr/README.md) |

[Full documentation index](docs/README.md) · [Design reference](docs/SIMPLE-DESIGN-GUIDE.md)

## Quick start

Use Node.js 22.13+ or 24+ and pnpm. Configure the Convex, Clerk and other integration values using [chapter 1](docs/chapters/01-getting-started/README.md), then:

```bash
pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
pnpm run dev
```

Open [localhost:3000](http://localhost:3000). A repository clone does not include the connected Convex database or hosted media. Public pages read Convex without Clerk; admin access uses Clerk and an owner allowlist.

## Stack

Next.js App Router · React · TypeScript · Convex · Clerk · UploadThing · Tailwind CSS and CSS Modules · React Three Fiber/Three.js · Vitest

The hero uses WebP stills and optional recorded video loops; live WebGL is loaded separately for interactive beach features. Exact dependency versions are in [package.json](package.json) and [pnpm-lock.yaml](pnpm-lock.yaml).

## Current work

The [change summary](docs/Change-summary.md) distinguishes local work from released changes. The documentation covers the beach version, including the current rendering, content, security and deployment boundaries; it does not recreate the original site's decision history.

## License and author

Code is available under the [MIT License](LICENSE). Third-party logos, photography, fonts and other media may have their own terms.

Built by [Chris Lane Jones](https://www.chrislanejones.com) · [GitHub](https://github.com/chrislanejones) · [LinkedIn](https://linkedin.com/in/chrislanejones)

boenchen1112/wafer-road.readme:
# 晶圓之路 Wafer Road

[繁體中文](#繁體中文) · [English](#english)

![screenshot](docs/screenshot.png)

**線上遊玩 / Play online: https://boenchen1112.github.io/wafer-road/**

---

## 繁體中文

**晶圓之路**是一款以半導體製程為主題的策略卡牌遊戲（適合 9 歲以上、2～5 人）。這是它的網頁數位版：可以和電腦對戰，或多位真人共用同一台裝置輪流遊玩，手機與電腦皆可使用。

打造晶片的任務開始了！你能率先完成晶圓的製程，成為半導體之星嗎？小心災難突襲——毒氣外洩、大停電、新進工程師，可能一夕之間逆轉戰局！

### 本機執行

```bash
npm install
npm run dev       # 開發伺服器
npm test          # 單元測試與大量隨機對局測試
npm run build     # 型別檢查並建置到 dist/
npm run preview   # 預覽建置結果
```

需要 Node.js 20 以上。部署：推送到 `main` 後，GitHub Actions 會自動建置並發佈到 GitHub Pages。

### 線上多人

首頁選「線上遊戲 Online」：建立房間會得到 4 個字母的房間代碼與分享連結（`https://boenchen1112.github.io/wafer-road/?room=ABCD`），朋友開連結即可加入，不需要帳號。房主可設定 2～5 個座位（真人／簡單電腦／普通電腦）、結束方式與回合計時（關閉／30／60／90 秒）；斷線或重新整理會自動回到原座位，輪到斷線玩家時由電腦代打。伺服器（Cloudflare Workers + Durable Object）使用同一份遊戲引擎，並且只會傳給每位玩家他自己看得到的資訊。

部署與設定步驟請見 **[docs/ONLINE.md](docs/ONLINE.md)**。未設定伺服器時，「線上遊戲」會停用，本機遊戲不受影響。

### 規則摘要

- 每位玩家有 2 片晶圓（第 0 階），起手 4 張牌；牌堆共 68 張（數位版採用模擬平衡後的配比，見 [docs/BALANCE.md](docs/BALANCE.md)）。
- 每回合：抽 1 張 → 打出 1 張牌**或**棄 1 張牌 → 手牌回到 4 張。
- 製程卡只能打在**自己的**晶圓上，且必須是剛好的下一階：薄膜 ×19（0→1）、微影蝕刻 ×8（1→2）、摻雜 ×7（2→3）、金屬層 ×5（3→4，晶圓完成）；晶圓代工 ×2 為萬用卡。
- 退回卡可打在任何玩家（含自己）的晶圓上，且晶圓必須剛好在該階：設備老舊 ×4（1→0）、曝光量錯誤 ×1（2→1）、離子佈植問題 ×1（3→2）。已完成的晶圓不受任何影響。
- 事件：大停電 ×2（所有玩家；沒有發電機者所有晶圓倒退 1 步，有發電機者改棄 1 張發電機）、毒氣外洩 ×4（指定 1 名玩家倒退 1 步，有逃生通道則改棄 1 張）。
- 災難：新進工程師 ×2（使對手棄 1 張發電機）、通道阻塞 ×4（使對手棄 1 張逃生通道）。
- 保護：發電機 ×3、逃生通道 ×4，面朝上放在自己面前，可疊加，每張擋 1 次對應事件後棄置。
- 功能：年終獎金 ×2 — 抽 2 張，然後打出 1 張再棄 1 張，或直接棄 2 張。
- 結束方式：**限時**（預設）最先完成 1 片晶圓者獲勝；牌堆用完則進行最終回合（每人再一回合）並計分（第 1/2/3 階 = 2/3/4 分，兩片相加，手上每張年終獎金 +1 分）。**長局**：牌堆用完時重洗棄牌堆，直到有人完成 1 片晶圓。

完整規則與卡牌圖鑑請見遊戲內的「如何遊玩」，以及依說明書整理的「製程原理」頁面。

### 專案結構

- `src/engine/` — 純函式、可決定性（seed）的遊戲引擎，無 DOM；`createGame`、`legalActions`、`applyAction`。線上多人模式的伺服器也運行同一份程式碼。
- `src/online/` — 線上通訊協定、玩家視角遮蔽（不洩漏他人手牌／牌堆／種子）與瀏覽器端連線。
- `server/` — Cloudflare Worker + Durable Object（獨立的 package.json／wrangler 設定與測試）。
- `src/ai/` — 電腦玩家（簡單／普通），只呼叫引擎 API。
- `src/ui/`、`src/i18n/`、`src/audio/` — Preact 介面、繁中／英文字典、WebAudio 合成音效。
- `tests/` — Vitest：每張卡的效果、保護、結束條件、計分，以及數千局隨機對局的 fuzz 測試。
- `scripts/e2e.mjs` — Playwright 自動遊玩並截圖（`npm run build && node scripts/e2e.mjs`）。
- `scripts/e2e-online.mjs` — 兩個瀏覽器的線上模式端對端測試（`SPAWN=1 node scripts/e2e-online.mjs`，需要先在 `server/` 執行 `npm ci`）。

### 製作名單

- 遊戲名稱：晶圓之路
- 遊戲類型：教育策略卡牌遊戲
- 設計主題：半導體製程
- 設計團隊：龔書宏、張容瑄、黃昱誠、陳博恩、沈虹
- 特別感謝：清華大學 洪秉驊
- 贊助單位：科林研發 (Lam Research) 半導體AI科學營

### 授權

程式碼採 [MIT 授權](LICENSE)（Daniel Chen (陳博恩) 與晶圓之路設計團隊）。**卡牌圖像、科林研發 (Lam Research) 標誌與品牌素材不在 MIT 範圍內**，著作權由各權利人保留，經授權使用，詳見 [ASSETS.md](ASSETS.md)。

---

## English

**Wafer Road (晶圓之路)** is a semiconductor-themed strategy card game for 2–5 players, ages 9+. This is its web version: play against bots, or pass one device around between several humans. It works on phones and desktops.

The chip-making mission begins! Can you be the first to finish a wafer and become the star of semiconductors? Beware of disasters — Toxic Gas Leak, Blackout and Rookie Engineer can turn the game around overnight!

### Run locally

```bash
npm install
npm run dev       # dev server
npm test          # unit tests + thousands of fuzzed bot games
npm run build     # type-check and build into dist/
npm run preview   # preview the production build
```

Requires Node.js 20+. Deployment: pushing to `main` builds and publishes to GitHub Pages through GitHub Actions.

### Online multiplayer

Choose "線上遊戲 Online" on the home page: creating a room gives you a 4-letter code and a share link (`https://boenchen1112.github.io/wafer-road/?room=ABCD`); friends join from the link, no accounts. The host sets 2-5 seats (human / Easy bot / Normal bot), the end mode and a turn timer (Off / 30 / 60 / 90 s). Refreshing or dropping offline rejoins your seat, and a bot covers a disconnected player's turn. The server (Cloudflare Workers + one Durable Object per room) runs the same game engine and sends each player only what they are allowed to see.

Setup and deployment steps: **[docs/ONLINE.md](docs/ONLINE.md)**. Without a configured server the Online tab is disabled and local play is unaffected.

### Rules summary

- Each player has 2 wafers (step 0) and starts with 4 cards; the deck has 68 cards (the digital version uses simulation-balanced counts, see [docs/BALANCE.md](docs/BALANCE.md)).
- Each turn: draw 1 → play 1 card **or** discard 1 card → hand is back to 4.
- Process cards go on **your own** wafers and only as the exact next step: Thin Film ×19 (0→1), Photolithography & Etch ×8 (1→2), Doping ×7 (2→3), Metallization ×5 (3→4, wafer complete); Foundry ×2 is wild.
- Regression cards may target any player's wafer (yours too) that is at exactly the required step: Aging Equipment ×4 (1→0), Exposure Error ×1 (2→1), Ion Implant Issue ×1 (3→2). Completed wafers are immune to everything.
- Events: Blackout ×2 (every player; without a Generator all wafers go back 1 step, with one you discard a Generator instead), Toxic Gas Leak ×4 (one player goes back 1 step unless they discard an Emergency Exit).
- Disasters: Rookie Engineer ×2 (opponent discards a Generator), Blocked Exit ×4 (opponent discards an Emergency Exit).
- Protection: Generator ×3, Emergency Exit ×4 — placed face-up, stackable, each blocks one matching event then is discarded.
- Function: Year-End Bonus ×2 — draw 2, then play 1 and discard 1, or discard 2.
- Ending: **Timed** (default) — first to complete a wafer wins; if the deck runs out there is a final round (everyone gets one more turn) and scoring (step 1/2/3 = 2/3/4 pts, both wafers summed, +1 per Year-End Bonus in hand). **Long game** — the discard pile is reshuffled when the deck runs out, until someone completes a wafer.

The full rules and a card reference are in the in-game "How to Play" page, plus a "Process Principles" page based on the booklet.

### Project layout

- `src/engine/` — pure, deterministic (seeded) game engine with no DOM: `createGame`, `legalActions`, `applyAction`. The online-multiplayer server runs this very same code.
- `src/online/` — on

WoodyWizard/SporeCoop.desc: Co-op multiplayer mod for SPORE (GOG): play every stage together — one shared world, your own creatures, co-op mechanics in Cell, Creature, Tribe, Civilization and Space
WoodyWizard/SporeCoop.readme:
☕ Like this project? Support the author on Buy Me a Coffee

**SporeCoop** is a multiplayer mod for Spore. Two to four friends evolve **in one world**, from the tide pool to the galaxy: everybody plays their own creature, the host's world is shared with the guests, and every stage has mechanics that only work together - revive a knocked-out cell, hunt as a pack, besiege a city from two sides, repair your partner's ship before it explodes.

## Contents - [Features](#features) · [Every stage together](#every-stage-together) · [Install](#install) · [How to play](#how-to-play) · [FAQ](#faq) · [Status and roadmap](#status-and-roadmap) · [Building from source](#building-from-source) · [Credits](#credits) ## Features - **Co-op from the main menu.** A *Co-op* item in Spore's own galaxy menu: host a game, find friends on your network or type an address, chat and get ready in the lobby. **F9** opens it in game. - **One world.** The host's save is sent to every guest and loaded automatically. The host simulates creatures, tribes, cities and ships; guests see the same world and act through the host. - **Your own creations.** Everybody plays their own creature, cell and spaceship from *My Creations*, and the others see it. - **Evolve together.** Entering an editor or the next stage starts a vote; it begins when everybody is ready, and the evolved world goes to everybody. - **Native look.** Windows, fonts and slide-in notifications use Spore's own interface. - **Safe for your saves.** A guest keeps the host's world in a separate slot; your own saves are never overwritten.
The Co-op window in the galaxy menu: host a game or join one. In game, F9: players, stage, ping, readiness, chat and your own creature.
## Every stage together | Stage | What you do together | |---|---| | 🦠 **Cell: Symbiosis** | One tide pool. A killing bite only knocks you out for 10 s: a partner who swims right next to you revives you, otherwise you respawn as a small cell next to them. | | 🦎 **Creature: Pack** | Hunt the same animals for +25 % damage; when you are about to die near a partner, the pack saves you; partners heal each other. | | 🔥 **Tribe: Chiefs** | The tribe's members are split between players, each with their own chief (+20 % aura). Attack a tribe from two sides for +50 % (a *pincer*), perform together to make friends faster, kill the epic creature together for 80 food. | | 🏙️ **Civilization: Governors** | Every player governs their own cities and vehicles and picks a role: military, economic or religious. Two players besieging one city take it 50 % faster; a city under attack calls the others; superweapons fire only after a vote. | | 🚀 **Space: Squadron** | Fight the same pirates in one system. A destroyed ship is only disabled for 20 s - a partner who flies close repairs it. Jump straight to a partner's star, get alerts about raids on their colonies, terraform a planet together. |
Cell. Bob is knocked out: Alice has 10 s to swim right next to him and revive him. Creature. Two players' own creatures in one pack, names above them.
Civilization. A city is under attack: every player gets the alarm and a beacon. Space. Bob's ship is disabled - a REPAIR beacon and a 20 s countdown.
## Install You need **Spore with Galactic Adventures** on Windows or on Linux with Wine (Bottles, Lutris, Proton). The mod is tested with the **GOG "SPORE Collection"** build. Every player installs the same SporeCoop version. 1. Download **`SporeCoopSetup.exe`** from [Releases](https://github.com/WoodyWizard/SporeCoop/releases/latest)

fix: loads never run inside Present; planet texture job guard; newer world transfer replaces a running one

Cause of the guest faults in a planet render while a world loaded (0xFB89D0, then 0xF9E660 /
0xF9E67E / 0xF9E6FE): a terrain sphere draws its textures in one-shot render jobs. The render
manager's frame (0x7604F0) takes the queued jobs, then calls Present of the previous frame (where
SporeKit's frame event and coop's on_frame run), then draws the taken jobs. A load started from
inside Present (a world received while the guest was in the galaxy menu, the host's coop.load)
left the galaxy menu and disposed its planets; the dispose could not remove a job the frame had
already taken, and the job was drawn with the terrain state and render targets gone. Repro: a
save loaded 0-1.5 s after the galaxy menu came up in fresh games, 4 of 17 faulted (old build).

* world.cpp: every load is queued (via_menu_tick): from a stage the quit message is posted only
  when the stage has been playable for 3 s (kStageSettle: the tribe setup 0xCD78E0 faulted once
  at 0xB12D32 with its simulator object [0x167FAAC] null, not reproduced), in the galaxy menu it
  waits kMenuSettle, and the load itself always runs outside the frame.
* gamefixes.cpp: the texture job's DrawLayer (vtable 0x14911FC slot 3) goes to a guard that skips
  the draw while the sphere's state or face targets are null (replaces the temperature call guard,
  after which the same draw faulted further on). Restored on unload; coop.status counts skips.

# Revision Escape Rooms (website)

The published maths, biology, chemistry and classical studies escape rooms, served by GitHub Pages. This folder only holds built games; the source for each lives in its own project folder next to this one (`Maths Escape Room`, `Biology Escape Room`, `Chemistry Escape Room`, `Classics Escape Room`).

## Updating the website

After changing any of the games, run from this folder:

```
./publish.sh
```

It rebuilds all four web apps, copies them here, commits and pushes. Use `./publish.sh --no-push` to rebuild without publishing.
