# Road to Life

The party-game version of the Road to Life Bible board game. One screen hosts (a TV, laptop or phone everyone can see) and everyone else joins on their phone with a 4-letter room code, like jackbox.tv.

## How to play

1. On the screen everyone can see, open the site and tap **Host a game on this screen**. Choose whether that screen is a player or just the TV.
2. Everyone else opens the site on their phone, types the room code (or scans the QR code) and picks Team 1 or Team 2.
3. The host picks a version:
   - **Board on the table**: you play on the printed board. The screens handle whose turn it is, the cards and the timer.
   - **Digital board**: no printed board needed. Roll 1 to 5 on screen; the number picks the pile. A right answer moves your piece one space toward the crown; first team to the crown wins.
4. Turns go back and forth between the teams, one person at a time.

Card rules built in:
- Only the person whose turn it is can show the answer.
- **Remain Dumb** cards are only shown on the screen of the person acting them out.
- **Who am I?** cards reveal one hint at a time. Guessing on the first hint moves 3 spaces, the second 2, the last 1.
- The timer starts with one tap (30s, 40s, 1:00 or 1:30) and shows on every screen.

## Settings (host)

- **Dice**: roll the on-screen die, or roll your real die and tap the number you got.
- **Remain Dumb cards**: hide them on the main screen (only the person who drew it sees it on their phone), or show them to everyone.

## Android app (phone as the hub)

Download the latest app: https://github.com/jwmap3/ROADTOLIFE/releases/latest/download/RoadToLife.apk

The app runs the game on your phone, and your phone is one of the players. Connect the phone to the TV (Smart View, Roku screen mirroring or Chromecast) and the app shows a separate TV screen with the board, the cards and the room code, while your phone keeps your own player screen. Everyone else joins from their phones on this site.

GitHub builds a new app automatically every time the game changes (see `.github/workflows/android.yml`). Every build is signed with the same key (`android/app/roadtolife.keystore`), so a new version installs over the old one and keeps the cards saved in the app.

## Showing it on a TV

- **Smart TV with a web browser** (Samsung, LG, Fire TV, Android TV): host from your phone, then open this site on the TV, type the room code and tap **Use this screen as the TV**.
- **Roku or any TV without a browser**: screen-mirror (cast) the host phone to the TV and turn the phone sideways.

## Files

- `index.html`, `game.js`: the whole app
- `cards.json`: every card, by deck (`lot`, `so`, `last`, `written`, `dumb`)
- `board.jpg`, `art/`: board and card-back artwork
- `vendor/`: PeerJS (phone-to-host connection) and a QR code generator

Phones connect straight to the host screen with WebRTC through PeerJS's free public signaling server, so there is no server to run. Most home Wi-Fi and phone networks work; a few strict networks block direct connections.

prasantkumarsahu/kalinga-lang.readme:
# Kalinga

A small "Rust++": simple syntax, classes with inheritance and interfaces, compiled to
native code through Rust. It relates to Rust the way early C++ related to C — the
Kalinga compiler translates `.kl` files to Rust source and hands them to `rustc -O`,
so programs get native speed and Rust's memory safety.

```kalinga
interface Show {
    fn show() -> str
}

abstract class Animal : Show {
    name: str
    init(name: str) { self.name = name }

    abstract fn sound() -> str
    override fn show() -> str { return "{self.name} says {self.sound()}" }
}

class Dog : Animal {                 // `:` lists one base class + any interfaces
    override fn sound() -> str { return "woof" }
}

enum Pet {
    Real(a: Animal)
    Imaginary(name: str)
}

fn main() {
    let pets = [Pet.Real(Dog("Rex")), Pet.Imaginary("Nessie")]
    for p in pets {
        match p {
            Real(a) => println(a.show())
            Imaginary(n) => println("{n} is imaginary")
        }
    }
    let counts = {"dogs": 1, "cats": 0}
    println([3, 1, 2].map(fn(x) => x * 10), counts)
}
```

Output:

```text
Rex says woof
Nessie is imaginary
[30, 10, 20] {cats: 0, dogs: 1}
```

## Features

- **Simple syntax**: no semicolons, `let`/`var`, `"string {interpolation}"`, type inference.
- **Objects**: classes, single inheritance, interfaces (which can extend each other),
  `abstract`, `private`, `static`, downcasting with `is`/`as`.
- **Data**: arrays, sorted maps `{K: V}`, optionals `T?` instead of null, enums with data
  and exhaustive `match`.
- **Functions**: lambdas, function types, `map`/`filter`/`sort_by`, generics.
- **Value types**: `struct`s with operator overloading (`pos += vel * dt`), stored inline
  like Rust structs — built for game math and numeric code.
- **Errors as values**: `Result<T, E>`, `Ok` / `Err`, and `?` to pass errors on. No
  exceptions.
- **Threads**: `Thread.spawn`, channels, shared values and `par_map` over every core.
  Only values cross threads, so data races cannot happen and single-threaded code stays
  fast.
- **Async**: `async fn` / `await` with a built-in runtime: timers, background jobs,
  `Async.all`.
- **Games**: `import "std/game"` for a window, 2D drawing, input, images and sounds (on
  macroquad), with Pong and Asteroids as examples.
- **Standard library**: `Math`, `Random`, `Time`, `std/math2d` (`Vec2`, `Rect`), `std/fs`
  (files and folders).
- **Modules and packages**: `import "file.kl"`; the `utkal` package manager for git and
  path packages, with per-package namespaces (`import "mathx" as mx`) and a lock file.
- **Rust interop**: call your own Rust code and any crates.io library with `use rust`,
  `use crate`, `extern fn` and inline `= rust { ... }` bodies — the way to graphics, audio
  and ML libraries.
- **Fast and safe**: compiles to Rust and then native code; no null, no unchecked
  indexing, no silent overflow, no `unsafe` in generated code.

## Documentation

The full guide, with runnable examples for every feature, is in [docs/](docs/README.md):
getting started, basics, control flow, functions, arrays and strings, maps, optionals,
enums and match, classes, inheritance, interfaces, lambdas, generics, structs, error
handling, modules, packages, Rust interop, threads, async, making a game, safety, tooling,
internals and a language reference. See [CHANGELOG.md](CHANGELOG.md) for what is new.

## Usage

Requires a Rust toolchain (`rustc` on PATH; `cargo` for crates and games; `git` for git
packages). Install both commands, `kalinga` and `utkal`:

```bash
cargo install --path .
```

Or run straight from the repository:

```bash
cargo run -- run examples/oop.kl
```

```bash
cargo run -- build examples/fib.kl -o fib.exe
```

```bash
cargo run -- emit examples/oop.kl
```

`emit` prints the generated Rust so you can see exactly what your program becomes.
`check <file> [--stdin]` only reports errors, which editors use for live diagnostics.

```bash
cargo run -- run examples/pong/main.kl
```

Projects with packages use `utkal`:

```bash
utkal new my-game
cd my-game
utkal add mathx --git https://github.com/someone/mathx --version 0.4
utkal run
```

## Editor support

A VS Code extension with syntax highlighting, completion, snippets, live errors, a Run
button and `utkal.toml` hints is in [editors/vscode](editors/vscode/README.md).

## Language

| Feature | Syntax |
|---|---|
| Variables | `let x = 1` (immutable), `var y = 2` (mutable), `let z: float = 1.0` |
| Types | `int` (64-bit), `float`, `bool`, `str`, `[T]` arrays, `{K: V}` maps, `T?` optionals, `fn(A) -> B`, classes, interfaces, enums |
| Functions | `fn add(a: int, b: int) -> int { return a + b }`, generic `fn first<T>(xs: [T]) -> T?` |
| Lambdas | `fn(x: int) -> int { return x * 2 }`, `fn(x) => x * 2`; named functions are values |
| Strings | `"Hi {name}"` interpolation, `{{` `}}` for literal braces |
| Control flow | `if / else if / else`, `while cond { }`, `for i in 0..10 { }`, `for x in array { }`, `for k in map { }`, `for ch in "text" { }`, `match`, `break`, `continue` |
| Enums | `enum Shape { Circle(r: float), Empty }`, `Shape.Circle(1.0)`, `match s { Circle(r) => ... }` |
| Optionals | `var o: int? = none`, `if let v = o { } else { }`, `o == none` |
| Classes | fields with optional defaults, `init(...)`, methods, `self`, `private`, `static fn`, generic `class Stack<T>` |
| Inheritance | `class B : A` — single base class; `override fn`; `super(...)`, `super.method()`; `abstract class` / `abstract fn`; `x is B`, `x as B` |
| Interfaces | `interface I : J { fn m() -> str }`, `class C : Base, I, J`; interfaces work as types |
| Modules | `import "lib/shapes.kl"`, `import "std/game"`, `import "mathx" as mx` (packages) |
| Errors | `fn f() -> Result<int, str>`, `return Err("...")`, `let v = f()?`, `match r { Ok(v) => ... Err(e) => ... }` |
| Threads | `Thread.spawn(fn() => work())` → `Task<T>`, `.join()`; `Channel<T>()`, `Shared(0)`, `xs.par_map(f)` |
| Async | `async fn load() -> int { await Time.wait(0.5) ...

commits.msg:
std/fs: files and folders

`import "std/fs"` gives `File` (read, read_lines, write, append, exists,
delete, copy, rename), `Dir` (list, create, exists, delete) and `Path`
(join, name, parent, extension). Failures return `Result<_, str>` with
the same wording on every system ("cannot read `x.txt`: not found").

Doc examples now each run in their own folder, so files they write stay
out of the repository.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Named arguments

`clamp(15, low: 0, high: 10)` and `Rect(w: 10, h: 5)`. Named arguments
come after unnamed ones and follow the parameter order, so arguments are
still evaluated as written. Names are checked against the parameters of
functions, methods, static functions, `init`, struct fields and enum
variants; struct fields with a default may be skipped.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

`while let`, `for i, x in xs` and inclusive ranges

- `while let x = value { }` repeats while an optional is not `none`.
- `for i, x in xs` gives positions with elements (arrays and strings),
  `for k, v in m` gives keys with values.
- `a..=b` includes `b` in `for` loops and slices.

Chapter 5 now covers slices, string indexing and the new string methods.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

`if` and `match` as values

`let x = if a > b { a } else { b }` and `let n = match d { Up => 1, _ => 0 }`.
Each branch ends with its value (a block may run statements first),
`else` is required, every branch gives the same type, and a `none`
branch makes the value optional. Statement and value `match` arms on
one line may be separated by commas.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Constants and static variables

Top-level `const NAME: T = value`, and in classes and structs
`const NAME: T = value` and `static var name: T = value`, used as
`Type.NAME`. Static variables are one value per thread, created on
first use. Values that depend on themselves are rejected.

Breaking: member constants were `static NAME: T = value`; the parser
explains the new form and `kalinga fix` rewrites it. std/game's colours
are updated.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Recursive enums

A variant may hold its own enum (`Add(left: Expr, right: Expr)`), also
through structs and optionals. Such fields are boxed in the generated
Rust and unboxed in match arms; printing and `==` work as before.
Structs that contain themselves are still an error.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Strings: indexing, slicing and text methods

`s[i]` gives a one-character `str`, `s[a..b]` / `xs[a..b]` slice with
bounds checks, and `str` gains split, replace, starts_with, ends_with,
find, code_at, chars, parse_int and parse_float. Adds `chr(n)`,
`args()` and `[str].join(sep)`. Strings cannot be changed in place.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

print without a newline, println with one, and `kalinga fix`

`print(...)` now writes its values without ending the line and flushes so
the text appears at once; `println(...)` ends the line and `println()`
prints an empty one.

`kalinga fix <files or folders>` updates code written for 0.4: calls of
the built-in `print` become `println` (found with the lexer, so strings,
comments, methods named print and declarations are left alone; files
that are not valid Kalinga are reported and skipped). `utkal fix` does
the same for a project's src/ and tests/ and updates `kalinga = ...` in
utkal.toml. The examples, tests, std modules, docs, README, snippets and
the `utkal new` template were migrated with it.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Whole-number literals where a float is expected

`Vec2(600, 300)`, `let w: float = 5`, `-3` as a float argument,
`speed * 2` and `x > 0` with a float `x` now work: a whole-number literal
is a float wherever a float is expected or next to a float in an
operator. For struct operators an `op` taking an int is still preferred
(`half * 3`); one taking a float is used otherwise (`v * 2`). Variables
still need `float(x)`.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Enforce function length and no unwrap in library code

clippy::too_many_lines (100 lines) is on for the workspace and
clippy::unwrap_used for the library crates (tests may unwrap). The last
long functions are split: named types get resolve_named, the namespace
rewriter gets `qualified`, and library calls split into Math, Random and
runtime (Thread/Time/Async) families sharing a LibCall helper instead of
duplicated arity checks. Remaining unwraps become checks the code states.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Add a registry of built-in functions and methods

kalinga-sema::builtins lists every built-in function, library function,
library constant and method of a built-in type with its signature and
documentation, for editors and docs. The type checker takes library names
and constants from it. Tests check both directions: every entry
type-checks when called with arguments of its parameter types, and the
reference and standard-library chapters list exactly the registry.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Parser error recovery

After a syntax error the parser skips to the next top-level declaration at
the start of a line and continues, so every declaration's syntax error is
reported. The 113-line top-level loop splits into item, use_decl,
crate_features and extern_decl.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Separate type checking from code generation

The old code generator checked types and wrote Rust in one pass (3,300
lines; `expr` returned both). Now:

- kalinga-sema::typeck checks every body and produces a typed tree
  (kalinga-sema::tast): each expression has its type, each name and call is
  resolved, each implicit conversion is an explicit Convert node. Error
  messages are unchanged. Bodies are checked independently, so all of a
  program's independent errors are reported (up to 20, in source order).
- kalinga-codegen prints the typed tree and can no longer fail. It is
  split into items, statements and expressions.

The generated Rust is byte-identical for the examples and tests (async
methods are now indented consistently). Every snapshot, documentation
example and crate/window test passes unchanged.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Split the checker into types, model and declaration passes

checker.rs (1,334 lines) becomes types.rs (Type, Signature, substitution
and unification), model.rs (the model and its queries) and declare.rs.
Model::build, one 464-line function, is now a sequence of named passes
(type names, enums, structs, value-type checks, interfaces, functions,
main, classes, class order, class rules), and check_class splits into
overrides and interface conformance. Checks run in the same order, so
every error message and position is unchanged.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Move the runtime out of a string literal into runtime/*.rs

The 420-line PRELUDE string becomes nine ordinary Rust files (show,
collections, random, threads, async_rt, channels, time, io, main), embedded
with include_str! and also compiled as a test module so rustc and clippy
check them. That found five lint issues, now fixed (slice parameters, a
type alias for boxed futures, a const thread_local, div_ceil). CI checks
their formatting.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Typed errors in the project and driver crates

kalinga-project returns ProjectError and kalinga-driver DriverError instead
of Result<_, String>; messages are unchanged. Compile errors stay
structured (CompileErrors: the diagnostics plus the source map they point
into), ready for editors. The driver's 113-line `load` becomes a Loader

# Analytics Intern take-home: Kevin

**Deck:** `EA_Analytics_Intern_Readout_Kevin.pptx` (slides 1–8 are the readout; the appendix follows)

## Headline findings
- **2(a) ARPDAU "down 16%":** nothing broke. ARPDAU rose in every country tier (+3% to +8%), but Tier 4's share of active player-days grew from 18% to 45% because of a paid_video install push. The mix effect (−$0.076) is larger than the whole drop (−$0.058). Gross revenue rose 2.9×. The real decision is Tier-4 CPI against a break-even of about $1.64 per install (90-day revenue after store fees).
- **3 Channels:** the naive −38% revenue gap for paid_video is an artefact of tier mix. Like for like it is −8% and not significant. The paid_video D7 gap (−1.3pp) is borderline and small. paid_social vs organic is below what this sample can detect.
- **4 Churn:** logistic regression with a time-based split. Test AUC 0.75, and the top decile churns at 2.6× the base rate. The offer threshold equals cost ÷ (uplift × value). 85% of players who go silent for 14 days return within 30 days anyway, so uplift has to be measured with a holdout.

## How to run

> **Data not included.** The five raw CSVs (player_profile, player_day, purchase, currency_spend, ad_view) belong to EA and are not in this repo. Put them in a `csv/` folder next to `run_sql.py` to reproduce every output. The two player-level output files (`outputs/3_channel_cohort.csv`, `outputs/4_test_predictions.csv`) are also left out; `run_all` recreates them.

```
# CSVs in ./csv/ or ./data/csv/ (or set EA_CSV_DIR)
bash run_all.sh        # Mac/Linux
run_all.bat            # Windows (double-click)
```
Python 3.10+, with DuckDB for all SQL (it runs directly on the CSVs, so no database server is needed). Rebuilding the deck needs Node.js + `pptxgenjs`.

| File | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `sql/00_setup_clean.sql` | Cleaned views: device→player map (linked devices), deduplicated purchases, refunds split out, ad_view shifted −8h |
| `sql/1a_daily_health.sql` | Task 1(a) DAU, revenue, ARPDAU, payer share by day × platform |
| `sql/1b_retention.sql`, `1b_weekly_retention.sql` | Task 1(b) cohort grid with censoring rule |
| `sql/1c_spenders.sql` | Task 1(c) concentration, time to first purchase, repeat gap (LAG) |
| `sql/1d_ads.sql` | Task 1(d) cap-hit rate and daily ad views |
| `sql/2a_arpdau_mix.sql` + `task2_arpdau.py` | Deep-dive 2(a) mix decomposition, value per install, LTV |
| `sql/3_channel_cohort.sql` + `task3_channels.py` | Channel comparison, bootstrap CIs, regression, MDE |
| `sql/4a_return_curve.sql`, `sql/4b_churn_features.sql` + `task4_churn.py` | Churn definition, features, model, thresholds |
| `task1_run.py` | Runs the Task 1 SQL, writes `outputs/` and `charts/` |
| `deck_data.py`, `deck/build_deck.js` | Deck built from `outputs/` (every number is traceable) |
| `exploration/` | First-pass profiling queries that found the data issues |

## Data quality issues handled
1. ad_view timestamps are 8h ahead of the other tables. Shifted back (after the shift, 100% of ad-days match an active day).
2. Ad logging outage on 5–6 Mar. Excluded and flagged.
3. 122 duplicated purchase_ids. Kept the first.
4. 226 refunds (negative rows). Excluded from gross; net reported.
5. 3,211 linked devices. Collapsed to one player.
6. 2,434 sale purchases on days with no activity (114 before install). Kept in revenue, excluded from payer share.
7. install_date is not first activity; 228 currency_spend outlier rows. Noted and not used.

Gkrumbach07/bwca-canoe.readme:
# BWCA Canoe

**Play it: https://gkrumbach07.github.io/bwca-canoe/** (a computer with a keyboard and mouse; about 20 MB
of map data streams in as you paddle).

**Watch the trailer:** [67 seconds, 720p, no sound](https://github.com/Gkrumbach07/bwca-canoe/releases/download/trailer-v2/bwca-trailer-v2-720p.mp4),
recorded frame by frame from the game ([`scripts/trailer/`](scripts/trailer/)).

[![Dusk on Lake One, from the trailer](docs/images/trailer-poster.jpg)](https://github.com/Gkrumbach07/bwca-canoe/releases/download/trailer-v2/bwca-trailer-v2-720p.mp4)

A quiet canoeing game set on real terrain in the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness: the whole
wilderness, from Crane Lake to the Pigeon River, streamed in 2.56 km tiles as you paddle. You start at the
Lake One landing (entry point 30) east of Ely, Minnesota.

- **Real elevation**: USGS 3DEP / SRTM heights via the public AWS Terrain Tiles (Terrarium encoding).
- **Real lakes, portages, campsites and entry points**: OpenStreetMap, from an offline Geofabrik extract.
  Creeks that OSM maps only as lines are water too, and rivers descend between lakes.
- **Real depths** where the Minnesota DNR has mapped the lake: its bathymetric contours shape the bed
  (85 lakes in the Boundary Waters, Snowbank at 43 m, Loon at 64 m); the HUD shows the depth under the canoe.
- **Real clarity**: every lake carries its mean Secchi depth from the DNR's lake data (272 measured lakes in the
  area, from 0.6 m bog water to 8.9 m at Clearwater; the rest estimated from their neighbours). Clear lakes
  are blue-green and show the bed far out; tea-stained lakes go olive-brown and close up within a few metres.
  The bed itself is coloured by depth: sand, shelf, weed, drop-off, hole.
- **Everything else is procedural**: terrain colouring, lake beds, nine tree species with per-tree variation,
  shoreline boulders, campsites (fire grate, log, tent), portage trails and markers, the canoe, the paddler
  and the paddle stroke, the water, the sky and the clouds. No external assets.
- **Streamed world**: a 10 m grid of 200 x 69 km (138 million cells) is baked into 2,106 tiles; the game keeps
  the 5 x 5 tiles around the canoe built (terrain, water, forest, lake plants, trails) in a pool of web
  workers, a coarse 80 m far field underneath, and lets the rest go.
- **GPS simulation**: the canoe's real-world latitude/longitude is broadcast as the device location,
  so other tabs that ask for geolocation see you paddling (see *GPS simulator* below).
- **The pace** (`src/pace.js`): a game day covers a real BWCA day's distance. Everything moves at life pace (a solo
  canoe at a tripper's 5.8 km an hour in strokes of about 1.6 m, a 3 mph walk in steps of about 0.7 m, a portage carry
  at 3 km an hour), and while you travel the canoe and the clock are time-lapsed together: at **Trip** pace (the
  default; Settings › Controls › Pace) ×4 on open water, a game hour of paddling in about fifteen real minutes, and up
  to ×3 on a portage trail, so a travel day of 4 to 6 game hours covers 20 to 25 km. The canoe's boost builds once the
  stroke is steady and eases off on a slow stroke, in a hard turn and in the last few metres before a bank dead ahead,
  but not along a shore or into a dock. Camp, chores, fishing and walking off a trail stay at life with the clock at
  12×. **Real** pace is 1:1 throughout. A "trip ×4" mark sits bottom right while the boost carries you, and the
  readout (Tab) gives the clock's rate and the km an hour, averaged over a stroke or two. The game keeps to the wall
  clock at any frame rate (a slow frame runs as several steps), so 5.8 km an hour is 5.8 km an hour.
- **A day in the Boundary Waters**: a day/night cycle on the pace's clock with the real sun and moon for the date and
  the clock (`src/astro.js`: sunrise and sunset shift through the year, the moon shows its phase), a
  sky-matched haze, golden light at the ends of the day, the clouds, the water, stars, with dawn mist over
  the lakes. The game starts on today's date at the current time.
- **Seasons** (`src/season.js`, from the day of the year): the lakes are frozen until ice-out in early May and
  again from late November; birch and aspen leaf out pale green in mid-May, turn gold in the last half of
  September and drop by the end of October, shrubs go red; grass goes tawny in the fall; lily pads are on the
  water from June to late September, fireweed blooms in high summer, loons are on the lakes from May to
  October, and cold mornings bring heavier mist. `day.season` carries all of it for anything else to use. Lakes are clear in the shallows
  (lily pads, reeds and weeds grow in sheltered water) and tannin-dark in the deep. Loons drift, dive and
  call; wind, lapping water and paddle dips are synthesized, no samples.
- **The look** (`docs/look.md`, after Firewatch): the ground is a painted splat of eight materials blended
  through world-space noise, so transitions are soft bands and never polygon edges; one smooth light model
  for everything (`src/shading.js`: Lambert, wrapped on the leaves, the sky as a hemisphere fill, soft
  stable shadows), with occlusion baked into every tree, rock and hull; grass tufts and fireweed near the camera.

## Run

```bash
npm install
npm run bake:all
npm run dev
```

Open http://localhost:5173. The game opens on a title screen over the live lake: **Continue** (or **Paddle in**
before any season) picks up the season saved in this browser (or starts one at Lake One), **New season** starts
one at any BWCA entry point, **Settings**
has the quality, sound and control options (applied live, kept in `localStorage`). **Esc** brings the
same screen up as a pause menu while playing. The baked map data lives in `public/data/` and is not committed (about 380 MB
of tiles); the first bake downloads the Minnesota OpenStreetMap extract (290 MB) and about 5,800 elevation
tiles (500 MB) into `data-cache/`, then bakes the whole wilderness in about a minute (3 GB of RAM). Re-bakes

# Courtside — private NBA & NBL stat tracker

A password-protected Next.js app that pulls live NBA and NBL (Australia/New Zealand) data from ESPN's public JSON feeds and computes the advanced analytics itself. A league switch at the very top of every page flips between the two; the app remembers the last one you picked.

## What's in it

| Area | What you get |
|---|---|
| **Dashboard** | League PPG, average game total, pace, offensive rating; today's games (live), next 7 days with betting line, O/U and a projected score/total; league leaders with headshots; teams ranked by average game total and net rating |
| **Teams** | All 30 teams + a sortable league table (PPG, OPP, pace, ORtg, DRtg, net, FG/3P/FT%, eFG%, TS%, OREB/DREB, AST, STL, BLK, TOV, PF, TOV%, FTr, 3PAr) with heat colouring |
| **Team page** | Overview with league ranks, four factors, team leaders, injury report; **player stats** (every per-game counting stat incl. OREB/DREB, turnovers, blocks); **advanced** (PER est., TS%, eFG%, USG%, AST/TO, game score, per-36); schedule & results with game totals vs league average; roster with headshots and bios |
| **Players** | Leaderboard by any category, qualified/all toggle, search, paging, any season back 6 years, regular season or playoffs |
| **Player page** | Bio + headshot, season tiles (PER, USG%, TS%), shooting splits, last 5/10 form, points trend, game log, career by season, shot chart + zones from recent games |
| **Game page** | Linescore, full box score, team comparison (paint/fast-break/points off TOs), advanced (possessions, pace, ORtg/DRtg, four factors, USG%, AST%, OREB%/DREB%/REB%, STL%, BLK%), **shot chart + heatmap**, shot zones (restricted area, paint, mid-range, corner 3, above-the-break 3), xPPS & shot-making, shot types, **score margin chart, lead changes, runs (e.g. 12–2)**, **clutch** stats (last 5 min ≤5 pts, last 2 min, whole 4th), **reconstructed 5-man lineups** with ORtg/DRtg/net, **live- vs dead-ball turnovers**, play-by-play and a possession-by-possession log; pre-game preview with projection, injuries and last five |
| **Tracking** | NBA.com hub: hustle, shot contests, Synergy play types (incl. team play-type mix), player tracking, defense, matchups, official lineups, clutch, advanced, scoring sources, shot zones — players or teams, any synced season |
| **Scan & combinations** | 'Scan for stats' on any game (or a whole day) scores every rotation player and writes a report; 'Build combinations' then simulates the game 10,000 times to estimate the most likely result, total, margin and multi-leg player combinations (points / assists / blocks and more), with a click-to-build custom combo |
| **Odds check** | Upload a screenshot of player props; names, lines and odds are read (Claude vision if `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` is set, otherwise free on-device OCR), checked against each player's last 10 games and projection, and marked Strong / Lean / Pass with our chance vs the bookmaker's (margin removed) |
| **Cricket · World** | Separate section from the league switcher: every match worldwide by NZ day (Tests, ODIs, T20Is, franchise and domestic, men & women) with format filters, live scores, full scorecards (batting, bowling, dots, extras), run rates, boundary %, chase maths and projected totals. Data: ESPN's cricket feed (ESPNcricinfo match data) |
| **Glossary** | Every formula, the league rule set, xPPS baselines and a data-coverage table |

### NBL (NZ & AUS)
`/nbl/...` is the same app — dashboard, games, teams, players, standings, scan & combinations, odds check, glossary — run on FIBA rules (4 × 10 min, foul-out on 5, 6.75 m three-point line drawn on the shot charts and used for corner-3 zones, pace per 40). ESPN publishes NBL box scores and play-by-play but **no season aggregates**, so team season stats, player averages, game logs, leaderboards and "stats allowed by team" are built in-app from every completed game's box score (`src/lib/boxSeason.ts`, `src/lib/boxSeasonCore.ts`). The first load of a season pulls each box score once; finished games are cached for a day. The ladder marks the top 2 (straight to the semis) and the play-in (3–6). NBA.com tracking (hustle, Synergy, matchups) is NBA-only, so the NBL has no Tracking section; ESPN doesn't publish NBL betting lines or headshots either.

### League environments
Each league is an isolated environment (`src/leagues/`) with its own rules (game length, OT, shot clock, foul-out, bonus, clutch window), stat definitions and data provider. All routes are scoped by league (`/nba/...`), so IDs never mix across leagues. Every timing calculation goes through `src/lib/rules.ts`. To add a league, copy `src/leagues/nba.ts` (ESPN season feeds) or `src/leagues/nbl.ts` (season stats built from box scores) and register it in `src/leagues/registry.ts` — it appears in the league switch automatically.

### NBA.com tracking data (via [nba_api](https://github.com/swar/nba_api))
The **Tracking** section and the **Tracking** tabs on player and team pages use official NBA.com data:
Synergy play types (iso, P&R ball handler/roll man, post-up, spot-up, handoff, cut, off screen, transition, putbacks) with PPP and percentile, shot contest level (closest defender 0–2 / 2–4 / 4–6 / 6+ ft), hustle (deflections, charges, contests, screen assists, loose balls, box-outs), who-guarded-who matchups, official 5-man lineups, official clutch, player tracking (speed, distance, drives, catch & shoot, pull-ups, touches, passing, rebound chances, rim defense), defense as closest defender, official ORtg/DRtg/PIE + estimated metrics, and season shot zones.

stats.nba.com blocks cloud servers (Vercel, AWS, Heroku), so this data is **pulled from your own computer** and committed to `data/nba/`. The app just reads those files.

```bash
# one-time
pip install -r sync/requirements.txt

# pull the current season and push (Vercel redeploys with the new data)
python sync/sync_nba.py --push
python sync/sync_nba.py --season 2025-26 --push          # a past seaso

# Portfolio

A vintage-scrapbook-styled portfolio site, built with Astro.

## Getting started

```bash
npm install
npm run dev
```

Then open http://localhost:4321/. Run `npm test` to run the test suite.

## Adding a new project

1. Add a Markdown file to `src/content/projects/`, e.g. `my-new-thing.md`.
2. Fill in the frontmatter (see any existing file in that folder for
   every field and what it means — `title`, `era`, `type`, `date`,
   `tags`, `cover`, `gallery`, `tools`, `links`, `featured`, `draft`).
   `era` decides which page URL the character appears on (a typo
   creates a stray page), and `type` decides which section of that
   page it's grouped under (shown in both the table of contents and
   as a heading).
3. Put its images in `public/images/projects/<slug>/` and point
   `cover`/`gallery` at them with paths starting `/images/...`.
4. Write the body of the file — that becomes the project's full
   write-up.
5. Run `npm run build` to check your frontmatter is valid (it won't
   catch a typo'd image path — open the page in your browser to
   confirm images actually load), then commit and push. Netlify
   redeploys automatically.

Set `draft: true` to keep a project out of the site entirely until
it's ready.

## The Living Portrait page

`/living-portrait` is a webcam-driven 3D avatar demo. All of its code is
in `src/tracker/` (plain TypeScript) and loads lazily — nothing heavy is
downloaded until a visitor clicks "Start camera", and the 3D/tracking
libraries (`three`, `@pixiv/three-vrm`, `@mediapipe/tasks-vision`) only
load after they grant camera permission. Nothing derived from the camera
ever leaves the browser.

Self-hosted assets live in `public/tracker/` (all committed to the repo,
served from this site's own origin, never a CDN):

- `avatar.vrm` — the 3D model (see "Swapping the avatar" below)
- `avatar.LICENSE.txt` — provenance and license of the shipped model
- `face_landmarker.task` + `wasm/` — the MediaPipe face-reading model and runtime

Type-check the tracker code with:

```bash
npm run check
```

## Swapping the avatar

1. Make or download a **VRM** model (VRoid Studio is free and exports VRM).
2. Keep the file under ~8 MB — in VRoid Studio's export dialog, reduce
   texture size (1024 or 2048) and enable polygon reduction if needed.
3. Replace `public/tracker/avatar.vrm` with your file (keep the name).
4. Update `public/tracker/avatar.LICENSE.txt` to describe your model.

# Portfolio

A vintage-scrapbook-styled portfolio site, built with Astro.

## Getting started

```bash
npm install
npm run dev
```

Then open http://localhost:4321/. Run `npm test` to run the test suite.

## Adding a new project

1. Add a Markdown file to `src/content/projects/`, e.g. `my-new-thing.md`.
2. Fill in the frontmatter (see any existing file in that folder for
   every field and what it means — `title`, `era`, `type`, `date`,
   `tags`, `cover`, `gallery`, `tools`, `links`, `featured`, `draft`).
   `era` decides which page URL the character appears on (a typo
   creates a stray page), and `type` decides which section of that
   page it's grouped under (shown in both the table of contents and
   as a heading).
3. Put its images in `public/images/projects/<slug>/` and point
   `cover`/`gallery` at them with paths starting `/images/...`.
4. Write the body of the file — that becomes the project's full
   write-up.
5. Run `npm run build` to check your frontmatter is valid (it won't
   catch a typo'd image path — open the page in your browser to
   confirm images actually load), then commit and push. Netlify
   redeploys automatically.

Set `draft: true` to keep a project out of the site entirely until
it's ready.

## The Living Portrait page

`/living-portrait` is a webcam-driven 3D avatar demo. All of its code is
in `src/tracker/` (plain TypeScript) and loads lazily — nothing heavy is
downloaded until a visitor clicks "Start camera", and the 3D/tracking
libraries (`three`, `@pixiv/three-vrm`, `@mediapipe/tasks-vision`) only
load after they grant camera permission. Nothing derived from the camera
ever leaves the browser.

Self-hosted assets live in `public/tracker/` (all committed to the repo,
served from this site's own origin, never a CDN):

- `avatar.vrm` — the 3D model (see "Swapping the avatar" below)
- `avatar.LICENSE.txt` — provenance and license of the shipped model
- `face_landmarker.task` + `wasm/` — the MediaPipe face-reading model and runtime

Type-check the tracker code with:

```bash
npm run check
```

## Swapping the avatar

1. Make or download a **VRM** model (VRoid Studio is free and exports VRM).
2. Keep the file under ~8 MB — in VRoid Studio's export dialog, reduce
   texture size (1024 or 2048) and enable polygon reduction if needed.
3. Replace `public/tracker/avatar.vrm` with your file (keep the name).
4. Update `public/tracker/avatar.LICENSE.txt` to describe your model.
5. Run `npm run build`, then open `/living-portrait/` and check it loads
   and tracks. No code changes are needed — the mapping drives the
   standard VRM expression presets (`blink`, `happy`, `aa`/`ih`/`ou`,
   `surprised`), which every VRM model has.

If a specific expression looks off, every tuning value lives in one
place: `DEFAULT_MAPPING_CONFIG` in `src/tracker/mapping.ts`.

## Manual QA checklist (run before each deploy)

- [ ] Resize the browser (or use dev tools' device toolbar) to phone,
      tablet, and desktop widths — layout doesn't break or scroll
      sideways.
- [ ] Tab through the whole site using only the keyboard — nav links,
      filter buttons, and the contact form are all reachable and show
      a visible focus outline.
- [ ] Submit the contact form on the *deployed* site (not local dev)
      and confirm the email arrives and the page redirects to
      `/contact/thanks/`.
- [ ] Run a Lighthouse audit (Chrome DevTools → Lighthouse tab) on the
      deployed homepage and note the accessibility/performance
      scores.
- [ ] Turn on "reduce motion" in your OS accessibility settings and
      confirm hover/focus effects still work but don't animate.
- [ ] On any era page (e.g. `/work/the-age-of-gods/`), click every
      table-of-contents button and confirm it jumps to the matching
      character section further down the same page.
- [ ] On `/work/`, click a project card and confirm it opens that
      character's era page (not a 404, not a different character's
      page).
- [ ] `/living-portrait/`: on a desktop, click "Start camera", grant
      permission — within a few seconds the avatar mirrors your head,
      blinks, mouth, and smile, smoothly.
- [ ] `/living-portrait/`: deny camera permission — the recovery message
      appears with a "Try again" button that re-prompts.
- [ ] `/living-portrait/`: click "Stop", then check your browser's
      camera indicator has turned off (camera released).
- [ ] `/living-portrait/`: while tracking, switch to another tab and
      back — camera indicator turns off on leave; a "Start again" panel
      is shown on return.
- [ ] `/living-portrait/` on a phone — it either runs (reduced quality)
      or shows a "runs best on a computer" message; it is never blank or
      broken.
- [ ] `/living-portrait/`: cover the camera / leave frame while running —
      the avatar eases to a neutral resting pose rather than freezing or
      glitching.
- [ ] `/living-portrait/`: turn your head left — the avatar's head turns
      to the *same* side of the screen (mirror, like a selfie), not the
      opposite. Same for tilting.

## Known v1 limitations

`PageLayout` currently uses a flat paper background color rather than
the textured/vignette background originally envisioned. The `Sticker`
decorative component exists in `src/components/` but isn't used
anywhere yet (`TapeStrip` is now used on the Living Portrait page).
Both are reasonable candidates for a follow-up pass.

The shipped placeholder avatar ("Rose", a CC0 model) has a minimal
expression rig — it supports mouth shapes, blink, and head movement, but
not `joy` or `surprised`, so **smile and eyebrow-raise do nothing until
you swap in a fuller VRM**. Any VRoid Studio export includes those
presets; see "Swapping the avatar" above. This is a limitation of the
sample model, not the tracker.

Armusss/geist-decompiled.readme:
# Geist matching decompilation (GITE01)

A matching decompilation of **Geist** (GameCube, n-Space 2005, NTSC-U `GITE01` rev 0).
The goal is C/C++ source that recompiles, with the original Metrowerks CodeWarrior compiler,
into a `main.dol` that is **byte-identical** to the retail one.

![progress map](docs/progress.svg)

Green = translation unit rebuilt from C/C++ byte-identically; orange = partly matched (C source exists and some
of its functions already compile to the original bytes; the unit still links from assembly); grey = still
assembly. Hover a square for the file name. Regenerate after a build with `python3 tools/progress_svg.py`
(run `ninja build/GITE01/report.json` first for the orange squares).

**Contributions are welcome**, from people and from AI models. You provide your own copy of the game.
Start with [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md). To point an AI agent at the repo, see
[docs/contributing-with-ai.md](docs/contributing-with-ai.md) (what to provide, setup, and prompts to paste);
agents should also read [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md). The work queue and what has been tried are in
[STATUS.md](STATUS.md), and the source shapes that make this compiler match are in
[docs/matching-tricks.md](docs/matching-tricks.md).

## Never distribute game data
This repository contains **no game data**. `orig/`, `build/` and all game binaries are gitignored. To build it you
need your own legally obtained copy of the game. Never commit or upload the DOL, REL, disc image, or anything
extracted from them, and never commit decompiler (Ghidra/IDA) pseudocode output.

## Setup
1. Extract `sys/main.dol` from your own copy of Geist (NTSC-U, `GITE01`) and place it at
   `orig/GITE01/sys/main.dol`. It must have SHA-1 `6612f52ce6c50bb831ffddd5264b22973304f288`.
   (`orig/GITE01/files/loader.rel`, SHA-1 `20cc25827a68208dd48e0929e901ef6a83feda42`, is not used yet.)
2. Install Python 3 and [ninja](https://ninja-build.org/). On Linux/macOS, `configure.py` downloads the rest
   into `build/`: decomp-toolkit (dtk v1.8.4), objdiff-cli, wibo (to run the Windows compilers), the
   CodeWarrior compilers and gc-wii-binutils. See [docs/getting_started.md](docs/getting_started.md) and
   [docs/dependencies.md](docs/dependencies.md) for details from the template.

## Build
```sh
python3 configure.py
ninja            # rebuilds main.dol and checks it against config/GITE01/build.sha1
```
A good build ends with `build/GITE01/main.dol: OK`.

## State
- **Libraries:** 201 of 203 units build from C and match: Dolphin SDK 77/77, MusyX 26/26, zlib 12/12,
  Runtime 8/8, MSL C 51/52, MetroTRK 27/28.
- **Game code** (CodeWarrior GC/1.3.2, C++) is split into 216 provisional units; file boundaries are corrected
  as files get matched. 54 are fully matched, each verified byte-identical in the linked DOL, and about 57 more
  are partly matched (see the progress map). STATUS.md has the per-unit queue.
- There's no symbol map on the disc, so names are descriptive guesses except for SDK/runtime functions that
  were recognised by signature. Placeholders are `fn_`/`lbl_` followed by the address.
- `loader.rel` is left out: its imports from main.dol use ELF-style section indices with absolute addresses,
  which dtk v1.8.4 rejects. It's only 10 functions and can be added later.

## Credits
- Built on [encounter/dtk-template](https://github.com/encounter/dtk-template) (CC0) and
  [decomp-toolkit](https://github.com/encounter/decomp-toolkit); template documentation is in [`docs/`](docs/).
- Dolphin SDK source in `src/dolphin/` and its headers in `include/` come from
  [doldecomp/dolsdk2004](https://github.com/doldecomp/dolsdk2004) (commit 2328b416), by TakaRikka, RevoSucks
  and the doldecomp contributors. That repository does not state a licence; all credit for that work goes to
  its authors, and they can ask for it to be removed or relicensed.
- MusyX source in `src/musyx/` is adapted from [AxioDL/musyx](https://github.com/AxioDL/musyx)
  (MIT, (c) 2023 Axiomatic Data Laboratories; commit ec4697520f70); licence in `src/musyx/LICENSE`.
- TRK_MINNOW_DOLPHIN, Runtime.PPCEABI.H and MSL_C math sources and headers are adapted from
  [zeldaret/tp](https://github.com/zeldaret/tp) (CC0; commit c8fa8c9, `libs/TRK_MINNOW_DOLPHIN`,
  `libs/PowerPC_EABI_Support`). Geist-specific edits: MetroTRK banner "v2.0", `__sys_alloc`, a new rand.c,
  time.c and time.gamecube.c.
- Parts of the MSL_C sources (string.c, FILE_POS.c, qsort.c, printf.c, ansi_fp.c, alloc.c) follow the
  PrimeDecomp/prime project (commit 4da6e0e, `extern/sdk/runtime`; no longer available at that GitHub address),
  an older MSL revision.
- `Gecko_ExceptionPPC.cp` follows the [projectPiki/pikmin2](https://github.com/projectPiki/pikmin2) decompilation's
  runtime source (CC0).
- zlib 1.1.4 in `src/zlib/` is from [madler/zlib](https://github.com/madler/zlib) tag v1.1.4 (zlib licence,
  `src/zlib/README.license`, (C) 1995-2002 Jean-loup Gailly and Mark Adler); K&R definitions converted to ANSI.
- The physics code in Geist uses the Open Dynamics Engine ([ODE](https://www.ode.org/), (C) 2001-2003
  Russell L. Smith, BSD licence); the matched solver and collision routines follow ODE's source as a reference.
- Geist is (C) n-Space / Nintendo. This project is an independent, unofficial reverse-engineering effort for
  preservation and study, and contains none of the game's data.

tsatria03/Mindsight-Windows.desc: A windows port of Mindsight, recovered from the iOS binary.
tsatria03/Mindsight-Windows.readme:
# Mindsight-Windows

A Windows port, in Python, of **MiNDSiGHT** (`com.lukecharman.mindsight` 1.0.2, by Luke Charman), an interactive audio adventure for iPhone that is no longer on the App Store. It is told entirely through binaural recordings: you listen to the story and solve the puzzles inside it by swiping up, down, left or right at the right moment.

The original was played by swiping, and every word it says is a recording, with no text to speech. This port plays the same recordings and takes the keyboard in place of the swipes, so it can be played entirely by ear, as the original was.

**Headphones are needed.** The recordings were made with a dummy-head microphone, so their 3D sound only works in headphones.

## Status

**Plans 1 to 5 of 6 are finished. The whole game can be played,** from its main menu, through every puzzle, to its ending and credits, saving at the original's checkpoints, with Continue and the dissertation from the credits. What is left is building and releasing it. The work is split into six plans, in `aidocks/plans/`, each written in full, with every question answered, before any was built:

1. **Reading the original: finished.** Tools that read the original's binary, a check of every puzzle value against it and of every recording on disk, and a plain-text listing of all 56 scenes in `analysis/script/scenes.txt`.
2. **The foundation: finished.** `Mindsight.py`, its logs, its crash file and its error message boxes, the timer loop, the screens, the fixed keys, the window's text, debug mode on the command line, a by-ear tool, and its silent tests.
3. **The audio: finished.** The recordings through pygame's mixer, the Solved sound, the pause clips, a buzz the game makes itself in place of the original's vibration (160 Hz, sine, at 20 percent, chosen by ear), and pausing when the window loses focus.
4. **The story engine: finished.** The 56 scenes and the original's rules, the menus included: the input lock, the cues and the buzz, every puzzle, failing and the Rewind's retry points, pause and losing focus, with five changes from the original, below.
5. **The menus and saves: finished.** The one saved scene, written safely at the original's checkpoints, Continue, and the dissertation PDF from the credits.
6. **Building and releasing: next.** `compiler.py` and `releaser.py`, with the story's recordings packed into an encrypted `data\story.dat`.

## How it plays

- **The swipes:** the arrow keys, or W, A, S and D.
- **The double tap,** which pauses and resumes: Escape, Enter or P.
- **Before the story starts,** in the menus, scenes 1 to 7, Escape quits the game instead, while Enter and P still pause.
- A key held with Shift, Control, Alt or the Windows key does nothing, so your screen reader's own commands never reach the game.
- **No speech, no settings, no volume controls.** The original had none of them; set the level with Windows' own volume. An error that stops the game shows a Windows message box, which your screen reader reads.
- **Pause** plays the original's pause message and holds everything; the swipes do nothing while paused. Switching to another window pauses by itself; coming back steps back 3 seconds and plays the welcome back, waiting for the double tap.
- **Saving** is the original's: the game saves the scene by itself at the story's checkpoints, nothing on quitting, and Continue plays the last one from its start. A new game clears nothing; the save is replaced at its first checkpoint.
- **The dissertation:** left on the credits opens the creator's dissertation, `MiNDSIGHT.pdf`, in Windows' default PDF viewer; coming back to the game plays the main menu.
- **Five changes from the original:** a buzz where it vibrated; swipes ignored while paused; the credits always following the ending; street rounds 2 and 3 buzzing at their cue; and a buzz as a scene begins only for the two loops, the guard and the piranhas.

If Windows can open no sound device, the game says so in a message box and closes, since every part of it is a recording.

## Requirements

- Windows, 64-bit, and Python 3.12 or newer.
- For the game: `pip install -r requirements.txt`, which holds `pygame` and `cryptography`.
- For the tools in `tools/`: `pip install capstone`. The game never needs it.

## Running it

From the repo root:

    python Mindsight.py
    python Mindsight.py --debug
    python Mindsight.py --debug --scene 47
    python Mindsight.py -v
    python Mindsight.py --exit-after 5

- `--debug` turns on debug mode for that run, from source only; the window title says "Mindsight (debug)".
- `--scene N`, in debug mode only, starts at scene N, 0 to 55, by the original's numbering, as if the scene before had just ended; that run never saves. `analysis/script/scenes.txt` lists every scene.
- `-v` writes a more detailed log.
- `--exit-after SECONDS` quits by itself, for the build's own test.

The game opens on the original's main menu, or with `--debug --scene N` on scene N. The window shows the scene, "Listening" or "Your turn", and "Paused", for anyone helping who can see the screen. The save is `saves\progress.json` in the save folder, holding one scene number; only one of the original's checkpoints counts, and a damaged file falls back on the one before it.

Every run writes `logs\log.txt` in the save folder, `%APPDATA%\Mindsight`, keeping the run before as `log.old.txt`. An error that stops the game writes `logs\crash.txt` there and shows a message box saying so.

## Tests

    python tests/suite.py
    python tests/suite.py keys runloop

The silent tests are in `tests/case/`, 126 of them in thirteen files: `test_paths`, `test_entry`, `test_runloop`, `test_keys`, `test_screens`, `test_mp3`, `test_recordings`, `test_audio`, `test_buzz`, `test_story`, `test_story_screen`, `test_jsonfile` and `test_progress`. Each file imports `_quiet.py` first, which gives it a throwaway save, keeps every message box shut, and uses SDL's dummy video and sound, so nothing is heard, nothing opens an

# あとで知ったこと

LINE風メッセージゲーム。主人公として自由に返信を書いて、相手はAIが演じる。
どの話にも主人公だけが知らない真相があって、会話の違和感に気づけるかが勝負。章ごとに評価が出て、最後に「あとで読み返すと」の答え合わせがある。

プロンプトの設計は [`prompts/README.md`](prompts/README.md) を見てね。

## 動かし方

```sh
npm install
export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-...
npm start          # http://localhost:3000
```

APIキーなしで画面だけ確認したいとき：

```sh
npm run mock
```

| 環境変数 | 内容 |
|---|---|
| `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` | Claude APIキー |
| `MODEL` | 使うモデル（デフォルト `claude-opus-5-5`） |
| `PORT` | ポート（デフォルト 3000） |
| `MOCK` | `1` にすると固定レスポンスで動く |

## claude.ai版（スマホで遊ぶ用）

サーバーなしで、claude.aiのページとして動く版もある。AIはページを開いた人のClaudeプランで動くから、APIキーはいらない。

公開中：https://claude.ai/artifact/Q8reYiUdYSMHiFVZWRMLsM （今は持ち主だけが開ける）

```sh
npm run build:artifact   # dist/artifact.html を作る
```

`lib/engine.js`、`artifact/backend.js`、`public/` と `prompts/` を1ファイルにまとめて、AI呼び出しをclaude.aiの仕組みに差し替えてる。
サーバー版と違って真相がページの中に入るから、開発者ツールで覗けばネタバレできる。ゲームの途中経過はそのブラウザの中に保存される。

## 構成

```
server.js          HTTPサーバー（/api/* と public/ の配信）
lib/engine.js      ゲーム進行の本体。サイコロ、状態管理、真相をクライアントに出さない処理
lib/game.js        サーバー版の保存先とAI呼び出しをエンジンにつなぐ
lib/claude.js      prompts/ を読んで Claude API を呼び、JSONを返す
lib/mock.js        MOCK=1 のときの固定レスポンス
public/            画面（素のHTML/CSS/JS）。backend.js はサーバー版のAPI呼び出し
artifact/          claude.ai版のバックエンドとビルドスクリプト
prompts/           AIへの指示書一式とサイコロの中身
data/history.json  遊んだ話の真相の要約（次のプリセットでかぶらないようにする）
```

## 今の制限

- ゲームの状態はメモリにしかないので、サーバーを再起動すると進行中の話は消える。
- 遊んだ履歴は全ユーザー共通（ログインがないため）。

amerikrainian/dicevoders.readme:
# DiceVoders

A [DiceVaders](https://store.steampowered.com/app/3917700/) mod that makes the game playable by
blind users.

Docs are [here](https://amerikrainian.com/dicevoders/)

## Install

Download `DiceVodersInstaller.exe` from the
[latest release](https://github.com/amerikrainian/dicevoders/releases) and run it. It finds
your Steam install, downloads the mod, and can later update, repair, or uninstall it. Manual
alternative: extract the release zip over the game folder (the one holding `DiceVaders.exe`).

The first launch after installing generates the loader's interop assemblies and can take a few
minutes; the mod says "DiceVoders loaded" once the game is up.

## Keys

Press F1, anywhere. It lists the keys that do something right where you are; Enter on a row runs
that key for you.

The basics are a screen reader's: arrows move, Tab and Shift+Tab cycle control groups, Enter
activates, Escape backs out, and typing letters searches the focused group. Ctrl+Shift+A hands
control back to the game and takes it again. Ctrl+Shift+M opens the mod menu. Ctrl+Left and
Ctrl+Right switch review buffers, Ctrl+Up and Ctrl+Down step through one.

## Building from source

```
dotnet build DiceVoders.slnx -c Debug                                # builds and deploys into the game
dotnet test src/DiceVoders.Tests/DiceVoders.Tests.csproj       # unit tests
```

Run `setup-bepinex.ps1` once first, then launch the game once through Steam so the interop
assemblies exist. A release is `build_release.ps1` (the mod zip), `build-installer.ps1` (the
installer exe) and `create-release.ps1 vX.Y.Z` (the GitHub release from a pushed tag and the
CHANGELOG section).

Runs on [BepInEx 6](https://github.com/BepInEx/BepInEx) (vendored); speech via
[Prism](https://github.com/ethindp/prism). The architecture, tooling and installer come from
[Guildrun Access](https://github.com/amerikrainian/guildrun-access); the installer is adapted from
the [Non-Visual Calculus](https://github.com/rashadnaqeeb/NonVisualCalculus) installer by Rashad
Naqeeb (MIT).

leftisthominid/lr-ffxiii-port.readme:
# Lightning Returns: Final Fantasy XIII - Triumfulgurate Edition

A builder for a native Windows and Android port, made from three copies of the game: Xbox 360, PS3, and Steam.

This builds a native Windows and/or Android version of **Lightning Returns: Final Fantasy XIII**
from **your own copy of the Xbox 360 game**, with what your PS3 and Steam copies add. The Xbox 360 code is recompiled to C++ on your
machine (with [ReXGlue](https://github.com/rexglue/rexglue-sdk)) and built into a normal game
program. Nothing from the game is in this repository: no code, no data, no art. Without your own
copy of the game there is nothing to build.

## How this was made

This decompilation / recompilation project was principally coded by an LLM (Claude, by
Anthropic). Another LLM (ChatGPT, by OpenAI) did the initial setup. The person who steered it
has nowhere near the coding experience it would have taken to do this without generative AI.

## What you need

- **The Xbox 360 game** (required): a disc image (.iso), the extracted game folder, or the copy
  an Xbox 360 wrote to a USB drive (Games on Demand / installed). It has to be the release as it
  is on the disc, without a title update (the builder checks `default.xex`).
- Optional, each adds something:
  - **The PS3 disc image** (USA, BLUS31311): the PS3 cinematics and the PS3 button / UI set
    (Settings > Button Prompts).
  - **The Steam version**: Japanese voices, lip-sync, and text (Settings > Voice / Text Language),
    and your Steam saves are imported.
  - **Xbox 360 DLC** (bought on a 360 or an Xbox One / Series console and downloaded on a 360,
    copied off it to USB): the DLC garbs and weapons.
  - **PS3 saves** (copied off a PS3, or from RPCS3): put the save folders in
    `Documents\lightningreturns\ps3_saves`; they are imported when the game starts (experimental).
- Windows 10 or 11, 64-bit, about 30 GB free, and an internet connection for the build tools.
- For Android: a phone or handheld with a Snapdragon (Adreno) GPU, Android 10 or newer, and USB
  debugging on. The builder downloads Google's Android tools itself, adb included.

## Status

Experimental. Built and played on Windows from the hand-made setup this builder automates; the
builder's own Windows build (360 disc image, PS3 disc image, Steam, 360 DLC) has run through on
one PC. Its Android build has so far only run through on Linux; the first Windows run is under way.
Known: the PS3 version of one movie (the ending, `ENA_us`) needs the latest builder.

## Use

Get the builder: **Code > Download ZIP** on this page (or `git clone`), and unpack it anywhere.

Double-click **`Build Lightning Returns.bat`** and answer the questions. The builder finds your
game files where it can, checks each one, downloads the build tools it needs into the output
folder (pinned versions, checked by SHA-256), and does the rest. A stopped build carries on from
where it stopped when you run it again. With a finished build, the same file offers to add the
360 DLC, the PS3 disc, or the Steam version later, or to install on a phone.

Your game files are only read, never changed. Microsoft's C++ build tools (Visual Studio 2022
Build Tools, "Desktop development with C++") are needed on Windows; if they are missing the
builder offers to install them (Windows asks for permission once).

To play on Windows: double-click **`lightningreturns.exe`** in the `Lightning Returns` folder of
the output folder (or the desktop shortcut the builder offers). Everything else is in the game's
Settings menu. The exe and the Android app get their icon from your own game: Lightning's face on the title
screen.

## What is in this repository

| Folder | What |
|---|---|
| `builder.ps1`, `builder\` | the builder (PowerShell) |
| `project\` | the ReXGlue project: CMake files, the recompiler manifest and function hints (addresses), and the port's own code (`src\`) |
| `plugin\` | the renderer (the ReXGlue SDK's graphics code with the port's changes) |
| `android\` | the Android app (Java, resources), the CMake wrappers, and the SDK's Android changes |
| `converters\` | the 360 unpacker, the PS3 UI converter, the Japanese voice converter, and the icon maker |
| `scripts\` | the 360 DLC / save importer |

## Credits

- **[ReXGlue SDK](https://github.com/rexglue/rexglue-sdk)**: the recompiler, runtime, and renderer
  this port is built on (BSD-3-Clause), itself derived from **[Xenia](https://github.com/xenia-project/xenia)**.
- **[bucanero](https://github.com/bucanero)**: the FF XIII-family save cipher (ff13-decrypter), the PS3
  save key derivation (apollo-lib), and the PS3 save tools (Apollo Save Tool, pfd_sfo_tools), which the
  Steam and PS3 save import follow.
- **flatz**: pfdtool, the PS3 `PARAM.PFD` format, and the save file decryption.
- **cp25stack**: Lightning Returns' PS3 secure file ID (via Apollo's `games.conf`).
- **Qualcomm**: Snapdragon Game Super Resolution 1, the Android upscaler (BSD-3-Clause).
- **AMD**: the DXBC checksum code (via Xenia).
- **Microsoft**: the GameInput header (MIT), for the controller's Share button.
- **Sean Barrett**: stb_image and stb_image_write (public domain / MIT).
- **Baldur Karlsson**: the RenderDoc API header (MIT).
- Downloaded by the builder, not part of this repository: LLVM, CMake, Ninja,
  [Real-ESRGAN](https://github.com/xinntao/Real-ESRGAN) (the icon upscale), ffmpeg (Gyan's Windows
  builds), Eclipse Temurin Java, MinGit, Google's Android SDK and NDK, and the third-party libraries
  the ReXGlue SDK uses (SDL3, FFmpeg, Vulkan headers, glslang, SPIRV-Tools, and others), each under
  its own license.

## Licenses

The port's own code: GNU General Public License v3.0 (`LICENSE`); the save import follows
bucanero's GPL-3.0 code. The ReXGlue SDK's license is in `LICENSES\`; every other third-party file
keeps its own license, stated at its top. Lightning Returns: Final Fantasy XIII is © SQUARE ENIX;
this project is not affiliated with or endorsed by Square Enix or Microsoft.

Boogs77/miniVIC_games.readme:
# miniVIC Games: 65C02 Arcade Collection

A collection of arcade games written in **65C02 assembly** for the **Boogs77-miniVIC**, a compact 8-bit computer built on the modular architecture of the [BO6502 System](https://github.com/Boogs77/BO6502_65C02-based_modular_computer). Every title uses the **TMS9918A** video processor for tile and sprite graphics and two **AY-3-8910** sound chips for stereo music and effects.

> 🚧 The **miniVIC** hardware project (schematics, enclosure, firmware) will be published in its own repository: [miniVIC_65c02](https://github.com/Boogs77/miniVIC_65c02) (coming soon). This repository contains only the game software.

---

## 🎮 Games

| File | Game | Players | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :---: | :--- |
| `tank.asm` | **Tank vs Tank** | 2 | Two tanks on a green battlefield: rotate, move and shoot. First to reach the winning score wins. |
| `1vs1.asm` | **1 vs 1 Basketball** | 2 | One-on-one basketball with shots, jumps, steals and blocks. 2 and 3 point shots, first to 21 wins. |
| `centipede.asm` | **Centipede** | 1 | The classic arcade: shoot the centipede through the mushroom field, watch out for the flea and the spider. Infinite levels. |
| `missile_command.asm` | **Missile Command** | 1–2 | Defend 6 cities from incoming missiles using 3 bases. The second player can join at any time. Full bitmap graphics. |
| `lunar_lander.asm` | **Lunar Lander** | 1 | Land the module softly on the moon pads: smaller pads pay more, plus a leftover fuel bonus. 6 moon maps, 3 landers. Full bitmap graphics. |
| `the_warriors.asm` | **The Warriors** | 2 | Street Fighter style fighting game: 5 warriors, 6 stages, punch, kick, block and special move. Best of 3 rounds. |
| `breakout.asm` | **Breakout** | 1–2 | Atari 1976: 8 rows of bricks in four colours, the ball speeds up and the paddle shrinks when you break through. Two walls, players take turns. |
| `asteroids.asm` | **Asteroids** | 1–2 | Atari 1979: vector-style asteroids that split in three sizes, large and small saucers, hyperspace and the famous heartbeat. Players take turns. |
| `space_invaders.asm` | **Space Invaders** | 1–2 | Taito 1978: 55 invaders that march one at a time, shields that crumble pixel by pixel, three kinds of bombs, mystery saucer and the four-note march. Colour bands of the cabinet overlay. |
| `warlords.asm` | **Warlords** | 1–2 | Atari 1980: four castles, shields on an L-shaped track, catch and throw the fireball. 1 or 2 players against the computer castles; first to 3 rounds wins. |
| `defender.asm` | **Defender** | 1 | Williams 1981: a scrolling planet that wraps around, scanner, landers kidnapping humanoids, mutants, bombers, pods, swarmers and baiters; laser, smart bombs, hyperspace. |
| `radar_scope.asm` | **Radar Scope** | 1–2 | Nintendo 1980: a field in perspective with a blue sky and a curved radar grid, 48 Gamma Raiders that hover forward, dive and drop decoys, and a damage meter that slows down the laser. Players take turns. |
| `space_firebird.asm` | **Space Firebird** | 1–2 | Nintendo 1980: a scrolling starfield, Firebirds that arrive as comets, loop the loop and turn into Gulls, Eagles and Emperors; eagle bombs that burst into shrapnel, a once-per-ship shielded warp and a PERFECT bonus for 50 birds out of 50. Players take turns. |
| `moon_cresta.asm` | **Moon Cresta** | 1–2 | Nichibutsu 1980: a three-stage rocket where every stage is a life, timed docking with retro rockets for a bonus and more firepower, and waves of Cold Eyes that split in two, Super Flies, Four-Ds, meteors and Atomic Piles, with a start tune. Players take turns. |

Each source file starts with a header describing controls, rules and technical notes.

> ℹ️ These games are non-commercial fan-made tributes to the original arcade games: see the **Disclaimer** at the end of this page.

---

## 🧠 Hardware Requirements

The games run on the miniVIC and rely on the following BO6502 modules:

### 📺 Video (TMS9918A)
* **Mode:** Graphics II (256x192, 32 sprites), bitmap mode for Missile Command.
* **Addressing:** VDP register port at **$B001**.
* **Reference:** [BO6502 VDU](https://github.com/Boogs77/BO6502_65C02-based_modular_computer/tree/main/BO6502%20VDU).

### 🔊 Audio (2 x AY-3-8910)
* **Right channel:** latch **$D380**, write **$D381**.
* **Left channel:** latch **$D384**, write **$D385**.
* **Reference:** [BO6502 AUDIO](https://github.com/Boogs77/BO6502_65C02-based_modular_computer/tree/main/BO6502%20AUDIO).

### 🕹️ Joysticks (W65C22 VIA)
* **Player 1:** PORTA at **$D581**.
* **Player 2:** PORTB at **$D580**.
* **Bits:** UP, DOWN, LEFT, RIGHT, button 1 (bit4), button 2 (bit5).
* **Reference:** [BO6502 JOYSTICK](https://github.com/Boogs77/BO6502_65C02-based_modular_computer/tree/main/BO6502%20JOYSTICK).

---

## 💻 Program Structure

All games share the same layout:
* **Load address:** programs are assembled at **$1000**.
* **NMI trampoline:** at **$0FD0**, called by the BIOS `NMI_HANDLER` with `JSR $0FD0` on every VDP vertical blank (60 Hz).
* **Frame update:** the NMI copies the sprite attribute table (SAT) buffer to the VDP and runs the sound engine, while the main loop handles game logic.
* **Graphics data:** screens, patterns and sprites are stored as generated tables at the bottom of each file.

---

## 🛠️ Build

The games are assembled with **vasm6502_oldstyle** (`-Fbin -dotdir -c02`). Ready-to-load binaries are in the [`bin`](bin) folder; each one starts at **$0FD0** (NMI trampoline) followed by the program at **$1000**.

To rebuild them:
1. Write the full path of `vasm6502_oldstyle.exe` in a file named `vasm.path` (or set the `VASM` environment variable).
2. Run `build.bat` to assemble all games, or `build.bat tank.asm` for a single one. In VS Code, press **Ctrl+Shift+B** to build the open file.

The script assembles every file into `bin/`, optionally copies the sources and binaries to the local folder written in `copy.path`, runs each game in the emulator to update its screenshots, then commits and pushes the

# Let's get creative: a starter AI agent

A small, readable AI agent built on Claude. You chat with it in your terminal, and it decides when to call tools to answer you.

The Anthropic SDK's tool runner drives the loop: Claude replies, calls tools, reads the results, and repeats until it has an answer.

## What it can do

| Tool | What it does |
|---|---|
| `calculate` | Exact arithmetic (a safe parser, not `eval`) |
| `current_time` | Current date and time in any timezone |
| `list_files` | List files in the agent's workspace |
| `read_file` | Read a text file from the workspace |
| `write_file` | Create or overwrite a file in the workspace |

The file tools can't reach anything outside the `workspace/` folder.

## Setup

Requires Python 3.10+ and an Anthropic API key.

```bash
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-...
python -m agent
```

Try asking:

- "What's 17% of 2,340, rounded to the nearest cent?"
- "What time is it in Tokyo right now?"
- "Write a short packing list for a weekend camping trip to packing.md, then read it back."

## Configuration

| Environment variable | Default | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `AGENT_MODEL` | `claude-opus-5-5` | Which Claude model to use |
| `AGENT_EFFORT` | `medium` | How hard Claude thinks: `low`, `medium`, `high`, `xhigh` or `max` |
| `AGENT_WORKSPACE` | `./workspace` | The only folder the file tools can access |

If Claude's safety classifiers decline a request, the agent automatically retries it on a fallback model (`fallbacks="default"`). Remove `betas` and `fallbacks` in `agent/main.py` to turn this off.

## Adding your own tool

Write a function in `agent/tools.py`, decorate it with `@beta_tool` and add it to `TOOLS`:

```python
@beta_tool
def get_weather(city: str) -> str:
    """Get the current weather for a city.

    Args:
        city: City name, e.g. "Paris".
    """
    return call_your_weather_api(city)
```

The SDK builds the tool's schema from the type hints and docstring, so write the docstring for Claude: say what the tool does and when to use it. Raise `ToolError("...")` when something goes wrong; Claude sees the message and can try again.

## Project layout

```
agent/
  main.py    # chat loop: talks to Claude and runs the tool runner
  tools.py   # tool definitions
tests/
  test_tools.py  # unit tests for each tool
  test_loop.py   # runs one full agent turn against a fake API (no key needed)
```

## Running tests

```bash
pip install -r requirements-dev.txt
python -m pytest
```

redconfetti/atoll.desc: Bikini Atoll: an SNES flight game in 65816 assembly
redconfetti/atoll.readme:
# Bikini Atoll

A Super Nintendo flight game, written in 65816 assembly. You fly a bomber across
the Pacific to Bikini Atoll, re-enacting the 1946 Operation Crossroads atomic
test on a fleet of uncrewed ships.

The ground is drawn in Mode 7, with a perspective matrix set for each scanline
by HDMA from precomputed ROM tables. The mushroom cloud is made with HDMA window
spans and colour math. Sound runs without an SPC700 program: the game writes
DSP registers directly through the APU's boot ROM loader.

## Screenshots

| | |
|:---:|:---:|
| ![Title screen](assets/screenshots/01-title.png) | ![Mission briefing](assets/screenshots/02-briefing.png) |
| Title screen | Mission briefing |
| ![Approaching the atoll](assets/screenshots/03-approach.png) | ![Target fleet in the sight](assets/screenshots/04-target-near.png) |
| Approaching the atoll | Target fleet in the sight |
| ![Bomb away, breaking away](assets/screenshots/05-bomb-away.png) | ![Shock wave](assets/screenshots/06-shock-wave.png) |
| Bomb away: breaking away | Detonation, seen from the tail camera |
| ![Mushroom cloud](assets/screenshots/07-mushroom-cloud.png) | ![Results screen](assets/screenshots/08-results.png) |
| Mushroom cloud over the lagoon | Results |

The screenshots were taken from a `DEMO=1` build with `tools/shot.sh`.

## Download

Get the latest ROM from the
[Releases page](https://github.com/redconfetti/atoll/releases/latest).

## About this project

This game was generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) as
a demo of its ability to make SNES games. The assembly source, the asset
generator, the build tools and this README were all written by Claude Code.

## Mission

1. Follow the red compass mark to the atoll.
2. Open the bomb bay.
3. Put the sight ring on the orange ship and drop when it reads OVER TARGET.
4. Break away: turn 155° before detonation.

The results screen shows how far from the target ship the bomb detonated and
how far you turned away.

## Controls

| SNES   | Keyboard (emulator) | Action             |
|--------|---------------------|--------------------|
| D-pad  | Arrows              | Bank / climb / dive |
| B      | X                   | Bomb bay doors     |
| A      | Z                   | Drop bomb          |
| X      | A                   | Change camera      |
| L / R  | Q / E               | Throttle           |
| START  | Enter               | Pause              |
| SELECT | ? or V              | Controls help      |

## Building

Requirements:

- [cc65](https://cc65.github.io/) (`ca65` and `ld65`)
- Python 3 with Pillow
- The URW base35 fonts and the Linux console fonts, which the asset generator
  reads from `/usr/share`

On Debian or Ubuntu:

```sh
sudo apt install cc65 python3-pil fonts-urw-base35 console-setup-linux
```

```sh
./build.sh                    # writes build/ww11.sfc
./build.sh build/atoll.sfc    # choose the output file
```

`build.sh` regenerates the graphics and data tables with
`tools/build_assets.py` when that script has changed, assembles
`src/main.s`, links it into four LoROM code banks, and then runs
`tools/mkrom.py`. That script appends the Mode 7 tables, pads the ROM to 4 MB
and fixes the checksum.

Extra arguments are passed to `ca65`, which enables these test builds:

```sh
./build.sh build/demo.sfc -D DEMO=1                    # autopilot flies the whole bomb run
./build.sh build/up.sfc   -D DEMO=1 -D DEMO_HOLD=JOY_UP  # also hold a button throughout
./build.sh build/alt.sfc  -D DEMO=1 -D DEMO_ALT=1        # alternate climbing and descending
```

## Releasing

Pushing a version tag builds the ROM on GitHub Actions and publishes it as a
release (see `.github/workflows/release.yml`):

```sh
git tag v1.0.0
git push origin v1.0.0
```

## Running

Load the `.sfc` file in any SNES emulator, such as Mednafen, bsnes or Mesen.

`tools/shot.sh` takes screenshots without a display, using Xvfb, Mednafen and
ImageMagick:

```sh
tools/shot.sh build/demo.sfc build/s 2 10 20   # screenshots at 2, 10 and 20 s
```

## Layout

| Path                    | Contents                                         |
|-------------------------|--------------------------------------------------|
| `src/main.s`            | The game: main loop, flight, HUD, sprites, explosion, sound |
| `src/snes.inc`          | SNES hardware register definitions               |
| `src/lorom.cfg`         | ld65 memory map (LoROM, 4 code banks)            |
| `tools/build_assets.py` | Generates the map, tiles, palettes, text screens and Mode 7 tables |
| `tools/mkrom.py`        | Builds the final 4 MB ROM image                  |
| `tools/shot.sh`         | Headless screenshot capture                      |
| `assets/screenshots/`   | Screenshots shown in this README                 |
| `build/`                | Generated assets and ROMs (not tracked in git)   |
